title: How Spiders Spin ‘Silk Dope’ Into Nature’s Toughest Material | Quanta Magazine
content:
MATERIALS SCIENCE
How Spiders Spin ‘Silk Dope’ Into Nature’s Toughest Material
By probing its molecular structure, biologists are uncovering how a tangle of unstructured proteins turns into a strong, flexible fiber.
Add as Preferred Source
(opens in a new tab)
i
A marbled orb weaver spider (Araneus marmoreus) builds its web one silk stitch at a time.
Konrad Wothe/NaturePL/Science Source
Introduction
By
Yasemin Saplakoglu
Senior Staff Writer
October 28, 2026
VIEW PDF/PRINT MODE
animals
biochemistry
biology
chemistry
insects
materials science
molecular biology
phase transitions
proteins
All topics
A spider, when knocked off a wall, doesn’t fall for long. Within milliseconds, it spins a soup of proteins into sturdy climbing gear. Using a thin, shimmering strand of silk, the spider hauls itself back up.
The strand is tougher than Kevlar, the synthetic fiber in bike tires and bulletproof vests, and stronger than steel. It’s flexible and biocompatible with human bodies. Scientists dream of making spider silk into high-performing materials for seat belts, helmets, naval materials, and even scaffolds to help repair brain cells. But attempts to make spider silk in the lab have fallen short because researchers don’t know enough about how a spider spins “silk dope,” a liquid blend of proteins, water, and salt, from its silk glands into a remarkable solid.
Mapping out the molecular mechanisms behind the process is “really the holy grail” for the field, said Gregory Holland
(opens a new tab)
, a chemist and spectroscopist at San Diego State University. Recently, he led research that described how the molecules in liquid spider dope reorganize into semiliquid droplets called condensates before turning into solid silk fiber. The result is an atomic-level look
(opens a new tab)
into the spider’s silk factory.
The findings are also a practical guide to the formation of condensates, which nature has used repeatedly to organize molecules for genetic processes and for the creation of impressively strong biological materials.
“It’s becoming clear that [condensates are] a common strategy that’s being used across a range of different organisms,” said Matthew Harrington
(opens a new tab)
, a biological materials scientist at McGill University who was not involved in the study. By unpacking how nature uses condensates, scientists hope to re-create some of its most rugged materials.
Silk Factory
Spiders are incredible natural factories. They can spin up to seven types of silks, and the same spider can often spin several of them. Aciniform silk wraps up insects for later snacking. Rubbery flagelliform silk reinforces the capture spiral to absorb shock. Dragline silk anchors webs and spiders to walls. Each type of silk has different properties depending on the species and related to how its molecules are assembled. And silks of the same type can have slightly different properties depending on the species.
In 1907, scientists discovered that spider silk is made of long, modular proteins, later named spidroins, which are in the same group of fiber proteins as collagen and keratin. More than half a century later, X-rays started to reveal the fiber’s underlying structure. The silk is made of flat sheets of protein, known as beta sheets, that are embedded in a less ordered, non-crystalline matrix.
Share this article
(opens a new tab)
Newsletter
Get Quanta Magazine delivered to your inbox
Subscribe now
Kristina Armitage/Quanta Magazine
In the early 2000s, as they inspected the spidroins in solution, researchers didn’t see organized, fixed structures like those seen in most proteins. Instead, the spidroins featured intrinsically disordered regions that fluttered around, forming and re-forming various shapes. Researchers then started to untangle how this soup of unstructured proteins could organize into strong, solid fibers.
One early theory suggested that proteins in the dope start to align with one another, as in a crystal, while remaining dynamic, in a transitional state known as “liquid crystal.” Another considered spider silk to be like silkworm silk, which has proteins organized into micelles, or small spheres, which then compress into silk fiber.
Then, in 2007, researchers noted that spidroins engineered in the lab formed liquidlike globs. Soon these kinds of structures would become inescapable in modern biology. In 2009, scientists at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Massachusetts and the Max Planck Institute in Germany discovered droplets of aggregated RNA molecules
(opens a new tab)
in fertilized worm eggs. These were condensates — liquid- or gel-like bubbles of concentrated proteins suspended in solution. Though observed for more than a century, condensates started to be seen as a critical organizational tool for molecular processes across life.
The researchers realized that condensates concentrate molecules, pre-organizing them into a flexible microenvironment without locking them in place like a solid. “Because they’re fluid, they’re malleable,” Harrington said, “so you [i.e., biology] can kind of shape them into whatever you want.”
A time-lapse video shows an orb-weaving European garden spider (Araneus diadematus) spinning its web.
Konrad Wothe/NaturePL/Science Source
More research showed that living cells use condensates everywhere, to organize DNA, regulate gene expression, and package proteins. At a macro scale, they help species build interesting materials. They help mold squid beaks into a gradient of stiff parts. They form strong adhesives that allow mussels to attach themselves to rocks, and marine cement that sandcastle worms use to build protective tubes.
“It’s been a hot area in biology,” Holland said.
Though researchers had described condensate-like blobs forming in lab-made spidroins more than a decade earlier, they weren’t thought of as condensates until 2020, when Keiji Numata
(opens a new tab)
, a biomaterials chemist at Kyoto University, suggested that spider silk undergoes a condensate phase
(opens a new tab)
during its transition from liquid dope to solid thread.
Condensates form by “liquid-liquid phase separation,” a process through which molecules in a liquid can start to interact weakly with one another, easily forming bonds and breaking them, as a result of a stimulus such as a change in pH, chemicals, or temperature. Numata proposed that phosphate in the ampulla, the middle section of a spider’s silk glands, might initiate these interactions. But no one had described the atomic-scale mechanisms that drive their formation until Hannah Johnson
(opens a new tab)
, then a graduate student in Holland’s lab, decided to take a look.
Inside a Black Widow
Every few months throughout 2023 and 2024, a package of female black widow spiders arrived at the San Diego State University chemistry department. The arachnids, jet black with a dash of red, cultivate a powerful venom that can be painful to humans. Except for that minor inconvenience, they make good subjects for studying spider silk. Their dragline silk spidroin proteins are some of the best-characterized in all spiders. And they’re available year-round, unlike some spiders that spin their webs seasonally.
To catch prey, black widows (left) lay a mess of sticky strands that acts as a trip wire. To collect silk for experiments, scientists gently reeled in strands from the spiders’ spinnerets (right).
Phil Degginger/Alamy; Courtesy of Gregory Holland
Six times over the course of two weeks, Johnson donned two pairs of protective gloves. Over the course of an hour, she and several students “silked” black widow spiders, which had been knocked unconscious by carbon dioxide. With tweezers, the scientists gently pulled the strand of silk from the spider’s spinnerets — the abdominal spigots that fibers emerge from — and reeled it in by winding it around a vial with a spinning motor.
“The spiders who give a ton of silk are our favorites,” Johnson said, “but I have a soft spot for the rebels who don’t want to cooperate.” Throughout the process, the researchers fed the black widows a cocktail of amino acids (like “protein shakes,” Johnson said) enriched with particular isotopes that they could detect in the lab.
Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy can map the structure of a molecule. It sends out radio frequencies to disturb the nuclei inside atoms, which then move in a way characteristic of the type of atom. Johnson used NMR on the liquid spider dope, as well as on condensates collected from the spiders’ ampullae. Meanwhile Kevin Chalek
(opens a new tab)
, then a postdoctoral researcher in Holland’s lab (now a researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles), mapped the atomic structure of the proteins in the solid fiber.
“We were trying to bridge the gap between what is happening when the protein is inside the spider and when it’s outside the spider,” Chalek said. “These are the same protein, [so] how can they be so different? And what exactly is happening between the two?”
Johnson observed that after she added phosphate to the liquid silk dope to start the condensation process, side groups on two amino acids (arginine and tyrosine) in the intrinsically disordered regions of the spidroin proteins started to interact weakly with one another. This interaction displaced water, organizing the disordered proteins into a denser, gel-like material — a condensate. The interaction persisted in the solid fiber, suggesting that the amino acids serve as “molecular stickers” that guide the disordered proteins into condensates and ultimately into fibers.
A scanning electron micrograph of spider silk spigots on a spiny-backed orb weaver (Gasteracantha cancriformis).
Dennis Kunkel Microscopy/Science Photo Library
Others on the team used AlphaFold, an artificial intelligence tool that models protein structures, and molecular dynamics software to predict this process computationally. Researchers know that spider silk’s strength comes from the sturdy beta-sheet protein structures in its final fiber. The team’s simulations showed that these amino acids line up right up at the bends in the beta sheets, suggesting that they are helping to guide the spindroins into their final structure.
“Understanding how those side groups interact and how they can develop structure that’s greater than the sum of its individual parts … is fantastic,” said Chris Holland
(opens a new tab)
, a biologist at the University of Sheffield who was not involved in the study and is not related to Gregory Holland. And they used real spiders, instead of synthetic silks, “which is brilliant.”
Their findings are “direct evidence” that condensates can form from native silk, which is “quite significant,” said Daiwen Yang
(opens a new tab)
, a biologist at the National University of Singapore who was not part of the study.
Their description of condensates doesn’t rule out earlier theories of spider silk formation. Gregory Holland, who had previously shown the presence of micelles in native spider silk
(opens a new tab)
, suggested that all three — micelles, condensates, and liquid crystals — could be stages of the same phase transition. Micelles that form in the liquid dope prevent the messy, disordered proteins from clumping and getting tangled. The proteins can also pre-assemble into condensates, or align into structures like liquid crystals before they are released from spinnerets as highly ordered fibers. But the actual process is likely “more dynamic and heterogenous” than sequential, Gregory Holland said, with several of these structures forming in the mixture at the same time.
Kristina Armitage/Quanta Magazine
Harrington agreed. “I don’t think these are mutually exclusive,” he said. “You might have different sorts of phase transitions that are occurring at different stages of the processing.”
Still, there’s more to understand about how these interactions add up on this factory line. There are likely other significant amino acid interactions that the researchers haven’t yet been able to map out in detail. They also want to look for triggers that initiate the process beyond phosphate. “There could be a range of other things that are driving structural changes in these proteins,” Chris Holland said. “We don’t know all of the switches yet.”
Superior Materials
Describing the entirety of the intricate silk-spinning process will take a lot of effort, but the payoff could be huge. Spiders produce small amounts of usable silk compared to silkworms, which have been reared for their cocoons for more than 4,000 years. It takes thousands of silkworms to make a silk shirt; it would take around 1 million spiders
(opens a new tab)
, in part because they don’t produce cocoons that can be easily processed. There is a more practical reason: Their cannibalistic nature makes them difficult to keep because each spider needs its own container.
RELATED:
Physicists Discover the Most Complex Forms of Ice Yet
A Newfound Source of Cellular Order in the Chemistry of Life
How Colorful Ribbon Diagrams Became the Face of Proteins
Why Insect Memories May Not Survive Metamorphosis
Producing spider silk in the lab could result in a new range of strong yet flexible materials. Kevlar, a synthetic fiber, is currently our toughest material, but it requires processing at very high temperatures and acidic conditions. “Here, you have an organism like a spider or a mussel,” Harrington said, “which is basically making a superior material under ambient conditions in seawater or in just plain air.”
Humans haven’t figured out how to match those organisms yet. When scientists synthesize spider silk in the lab, using the exact sequence of amino acids to build a spidroin protein, the resulting silk is not as strong as natural silk. “Something is happening there that we’re also struggling to mimic,” Chalek said. He thinks additional strength must be provided by something beyond the protein’s beta sheets, arising from other aspects of silk’s structure, or perhaps from parts of the spidroin protein frequently left out of synthetic silk solutions.
“I think once we really understand those blueprints,” Chris Holland said, “we’ll be able to do more stuff with silk.”

Build around your workflow
Define everything in code
Deploy agents wherever you need them
Get started
Software teams use agents defined as code to handle recurring work across the development lifecycle. These agents connect to the places where a team works and act when relevant events occur, whether that means reviewing a pull request, executing a compliance workflow, or investigating an incident.
The most useful agents are tailored to how a particular team operates. Until now, building one has generally meant adopting a product designed around someone else's workflow or starting from scratch.
Today, we're releasing the Agent SDK, the framework we use to build our own managed agents like Bugbot, Security Reviewer, and Rollouts. Agent SDK allows you to define agents in code and manage them like any other software project. Start from a template or point your coding agent at our docs. When the agent is ready, agent-sdk deploy it to Cursor infrastructure with one command.
Build around your workflow
The Agent SDK lets you quickly build and deploy agents that work the way your team does. They respond to the events your team already handles and follow policies your team can inspect and change.
Code review is one example. Each team has its own standards for what requires attention and who should review it. With the Agent SDK, you can build an agent that responds to pull request events from GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The agent can assess the risk of a change, route it to the right team, and approve changes that meet your policy.
As an example, a team within Cursor had built a large, fast-growing knowledge base of lessons learned and wanted every pull request checked against it. This way, the team's past decisions would hold even as the codebase changed. With the Agent SDK, they built kb-reviewer in about a day. It now runs on every PR in their main codebase, flags changes that contradict a recorded lesson, cites the note behind each finding, and encourages engineers to reconcile the discrepancies it reports.
For more complicated work, agents can hand a task to another specialized agent with its own tools and sessions. They can also divide a job among subagents working in parallel.
The Agent SDK also supports evals and event replay out of the box, allowing for rapid development with assurances that critical workflows execute the way you expect. The PGA Tour uses the Agent SDK to power their software development factory. Evals keep them moving quickly.
The Agent SDK has enabled PGA to build every component of our software factory on Cursor's infrastructure. It provides the flexibility we need to build agents that drive our development process. And built-in support for evals allows us to quickly iterate on new ideas and optimize existing capabilities reliably.
Michael Gyarmathy
Principal Engineer, PGA America
Define everything in code
An Agent SDK agent is organized like a small software project. The instructions that guide it sit alongside code for its tools, connections to outside services, and the evals used to test it.
Each file represents something the agent knows or can do. Prompts are written in Markdown, while tools are defined as TypeScript functions. Because everything is code, changes can go through the same version control and review process as the rest of your software.
Deploy agents wherever you need them
When you're ready to put an agent into use, you can deploy it to Cursor by running agent-sdk deploy from the project directory. The command builds the agent, gives it a URL, and starts it on our infrastructure. You can manage secrets and integrations from the dashboard, while continuing to use the same logs, evals, and playground available locally.
You can also run the agent on your own infrastructure. Each agent runs as a single Node process that can be packaged in a container.
Get started
Getting started with the Agent SDK looks much like starting any other software project. Create a project directory, then launch the local playground:
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { defineAgent } from "@cursor/agent-sdk";

export default defineAgent({
  name: "Robo",
  model: {
    id: "composer-2.5",
    params: [
      { id: "effort", value: "high" },
      { id: "fast", value: "true" },
    ],
  },
  local: {
    cwd: join(homedir(), ".cache", "factory", "robo"),
  },
})
From there, you can iterate locally and run evals before deploying with agent-sdk deploy.
The Agent SDK also ships with skills that guide coding agents through the development process. You can point an agent at the docs and have it help build the bot with you.
The Agent SDK is generally available today. Read the docs and get started.

title: EMACS turns 50 | MIT Technology Review
content:
MIT ALUMNI NEWS: 1865
EMACS turns 50
How the MIT AI Lab’s text editor gave birth to the free software movement.
By Simson Garfinkel ’87, PhD ’05
archive page
October 20, 2026
Artwork from Richard Stallman’s 1981 EMACS manual. Later iterations of the manual featured cover art of a medieval knight riding a yak. The complex yet playful illustrations captured the hacker culture of the era.
INTERNET ARCHIVE
Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards. 
A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code. 
By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display.
One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used. 
EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system.
EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code. 
In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time. 
“Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.”
Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74
Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT AI Lab, saw a full-screen editor—called E—on a visit to Stanford’s AI Lab. Inspired, he returned to MIT and set out to improve Control-R. The most important change to the program’s underlying structure: Every key ran its own macro when pressed, making Control-R far easier to customize. The lab’s hackers took to Stallman’s code with gusto and started changing and adding commands. 
That created an issue for Guy Steele Jr., SM ’77, PhD ’80. A graduate student in the lab, Steele frequently needed to help other lab members debug their programs. “I noticed that it was much harder for me to help someone who was using one of these packages rather than straight TECO,” he recalls. “Eventually, it occurred to me to try [to] broker consensus on a standard set of Control-R commands that everyone could agree to use.”
David Moon ’75, another member of the lab, helped out. Stallman jumped in as well, and eventually he took over. Together, the group assigned a standard set of commands that made use of the Meta key found on many of the lab’s early keyboards: Meta-F would move the cursor forward a word, Meta-B would move it back a word, and so on. They called the result EMACS, short for “Editor Macros” or “Editing Macros.” “My goal was not to construct a great new text editor,” says Steele. “I was trying to address a social problem.”
Nevertheless, EMACS was a great new text editor. Whereas Control-R could be tricky, EMACS users with “no technical experience at all” could learn to edit letters, emails, and even programs “within minutes or an hour,” according to a history by Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74. Meanwhile, “experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.”
Stallman started distributing EMACS to anyone who sent him a magnetic tape and a postage-paid return envelope. “EMACS does not cost anything; instead, you are joining the EMACS software-sharing commune,” he wrote in the 1981 manual. “The conditions of membership are that you must send back any improvements you make to EMACS.” 
Programming manuals for the Multics operating system. While working at Honeywell, Bernard S. Greenberg wrote his own version of EMACS for the system. It was so good, Honeywell commercialized it.
MIT MUSEUM
Greenberg, meanwhile, decided to write his own version for Multics, an early operating system by that time owned by his employer, Honeywell. Greenberg’s EMACS won first prize at the International Honeywell Software Conference in 1980, and Honeywell started selling it. Honeywell wasn’t alone in marketing a version of EMACS: James Arthur Gosling, a Carnegie Mellon graduate who went on to lead the development of the Java programming language, made a version that he eventually sold as a commercial product. 
This transition from free to paid software ultimately spurred Stallman to launch a project to create an operating system that could be freely shared and improved by its users. He modeled this effort, called the GNU Project, after the increasingly popular Unix operating system from Bell Labs. “GNU” was short for “GNU’s Not Unix,” alluding to the fact that, unlike Unix, it would be free. 
The project’s first major application was GNU Emacs (now restyled in lowercase). The GNU/Linux operating system was still years away, so, despite the project’s aim to create an entirely free operating system, GNU Emacs initally ran on Unix. It would eventually run on a range of operating systems, including Linux but also other Unix-based systems. When Apple launched Mac OS X, the first release of its Unix-based operating system, in 2001, GNU Emacs was included.
Apple stopped shipping GNU Emacs in 2019, but the company still has a program called mg (“Micro GNU Emacs”). Though it supports most EMACS commands, it lacks an integrated programming language, making it what some call an “ersatz EMACS.” 
Meanwhile, much of Apple’s OS still has hidden support for EMACS commands. The keyboard has no Meta key, but Control-Option-B will move back one word, and Control-Option-F will move one forward. 
by Simson Garfinkel ’87, PhD ’05

title: Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5 - Divyansh Agrawal
content:
← My writing
COMPILED WEIGHTS
Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
A stock Qwen 3.5 4B with a RISC-V CPU compiled into its weights, running on its own Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM.
BY DIVYANSH AGRAWAL
22 OCTOBER 2026
9 MIN READ
MARKDOWN VERSION
👏
...
Save
ON THIS PAGE
I can't believe it's not silicon
The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM
Compiling a computer into layers
The CPU
How Qwen uses it
Does it work?
A hard drive? In this economy?
Limits and what's next
Beyond arithmetic
Try it
I can't believe it's not silicon
Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide.) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever.
To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage.
I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring, and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with.
QWEN HANDS A MULTIPLICATION TO THE RISC-V CPU INSIDE ITS OWN WEIGHTS; THE CPU'S RAM IS GATED DELTANET STATE
You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope, and the code is on GitHub.
The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM
Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism (more on that here). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated.
Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1,1
1 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades.
the write strength (beta) to 1,2
2 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended.
and using one-hot key encoding,3
3 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell.
every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache.
GATED DELTANET STATE USED AS RAM: A ONE-HOT KEY OVERWRITES ONE ROW, A ONE-HOT QUERY READS IT BACK, AND THE CPU KEEPS ITS REGISTERS, MEMORY AND PROGRAM COUNTER IN THOSE ROWS
The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. (2021) showed that linear attention with the delta rule works as an associative memory, or "fast weights".4
4 Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, "Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers", ICML 2021.
The new thing here is making it exact and addressable, inside a production model, reliably enough to run a whole CPU on it.
This is the base on which this entire model is built. As it stands, default Qwen 3.5 does not keep exact values in the GDN. With this modification, we unlock the next part of this experiment.
Compiling a computer into layers
Since we have a fully functional, cheap and fast RAM now, we can go ahead with compiling a working CPU into the model weights. Luckily, there's no training involved: a compiler sets every weight directly. You describe the CPU as a circuit, a long list of small steps like "read this register", "add these two numbers" or "jump if zero", and the compiler turns each step into a piece of a transformer layer: attention heads that look things up, feed-forward units that do the arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads that hold the RAM. The CPU then runs as the model decodes.
Each instruction becomes a few generated tokens: one names the memory row to write (ADDR), the next carries the value (VAL), and a STEP token ends the instruction. Those tokens are the CPU's execution trace, so while Qwen is generating them, the CPU is actually running.
The CPU
The CPU is a 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IM, plus the Zba extension and a small bignum unit for big-number arithmetic), and it takes up 11 layers in front of Qwen's 32. As it stands, it passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error.5
5 Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps.
This CPU can also run C and MicroPython code in the forward passes quite well (although a bit slowly). It is not a Linux-class chip yet, but it implements the full RV32IM instruction set.
How Qwen uses it
Qwen 3.5 4B is able to use this CPU quite well, without any post-training required. The CPU is used completely internally, and not invoked through any external tool calls.
In order to make the model use this reliably, I decided to go the cheap way: by piggybacking on the tool call format that models are quite well-trained on, Qwen sends the CPU its instructions and reads back the results. No external tool calls or runtime are used. Once our CPU receives the instructions, the computer layers run, and then write the tool response. We use a small driver called RvChat to load the firmware into the GDN state, and this keeps the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers.
Qwen's original weights stay exactly as they are. The computer weights are added on top of them, in extra dims and layers.
Does it work?
I think the main question here on your mind after reading through my incessant ranting will be: does this actually work?
ACCURACY OF BASE QWEN3.5-4B, QWENPUTER AND BASE QWEN WITH A PYTHON TOOL ON NUPA AND DEEPMIND ARITHMETIC SETS
On the DeepMind sets:
div_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 95% by giving Qwen 3.5 4B a Python tool and 72.5% for base Qwen.
mul_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, versus 100% with a Python tool and 55% for base Qwen.
mul_div_multiple_longer: Qwenputer scores 100%, versus 97.5% with a Python tool and 90% for base Qwen.
add_or_sub_big: Qwenputer scores 97.5%, the same as with a Python tool, and 87.5% for base Qwen.
On NUPA's long-integer arithmetic, Qwenputer goes from 48.6% to 100%, the same as giving Qwen a Python tool.
The numbers the CPU prints are exact, too: I replayed about 230,000 of its output positions against a reference machine and found zero mismatches. And bolting a computer onto Qwen doesn't change how it talks: its normal text stays within noise of base Qwen (KL 6e-4, against a noise floor of 5e-4).
A hard drive? In this economy?
Because a CPU inside a language model clearly wasn't cursed enough, I decided the prudent thing would be to give it a filesystem too.
Since we already have a functional RAM, this was mostly trivial. On the model side, it's exposed via internal put / append / get / list / delete operations. Once again, no actual tool calls. When Qwen 'saves' a file, the compiled layers hash its name into one of 1,024 slots in a directory kept in the DeltaNet state, and store the text itself in other heads, with eight tokens per row, chained together. In scenarios where two names end up landing on the same slot, it just checks the next one. Finding a file again takes roughly two or three steps instead of a scan, and it holds up to 512 files, which comes out to about 53,000 tokens of text.
Fun thing is, this is quite persistent. You can save the state at the end of a conversation, load it into the next one, and the files are still there. Using this filesystem, Qwen gets facts that changed between chats right 90% of the time, against 30% when you paste the old chats back in, and it's on par with giving Qwen memory tools run by Python (83.3% vs 78.9%). This one is still experimental, and its code lives on the rv-store branch, with the model on Hugging Face and ModelScope.
Limits and what's next
Qwenputer is very much an experiment, so a few limitations. The extra layers and wider hidden size make the checkpoint 18.8 GB, roughly double base Qwen, although most of it is zero padding. It also needs a small driver (RvChat) to boot the firmware and keep the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers, so it doesn't run with a plain generate() call yet. And it's a bit slow, with every CPU instruction costing a few decoded tokens, so a big calculation takes seconds rather than milliseconds. The batched executor I used for the benchmarks runs about 3,200 CPU tokens a second on an L4.
Next up, I want Qwen to write Python and run it on the MicroPython inside its own weights, through a python() tool that works the same way calc does. Making the CPU faster is the other big one.
Beyond arithmetic
Exact control over the RNN layers is useful for a lot more than arithmetic. It also makes Qwenputer a really nice testbed for AI safety research, and I wrote up two follow-ups: how hybrid models like Qwen 3.5 can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring, and how compiled weights can work as monitorability tools, like an in-weight monitor the model can't switch off, or answer keys for interpretability.
Try it
If you want to play with it yourself, the model runs on a single 24 GB GPU. You'll need uv and the Hugging Face CLI. You don't need a tool server or a Python sandbox for the calculations: the CPU runs them inside the model.
git clone https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer && cd qwenputer/experimental/riscv && uv sync --extra hf
hf download divagr1925/Qwen3.5-4B-Qwenputer --local-dir qwenputer-rv
uv run python -m chipformer.rv.chat qwenputer-rv --firmware tests/data/rv/calc-bridge.elf \
    --ask "Use calc: what is 123456789 * 987654321?"
Everything is open: the code on GitHub, and both models on Hugging Face (Qwenputer, Filesystem) and ModelScope (Qwenputer, Filesystem).
If you use it in your work, you can cite it as:
@software{agrawal2026qwenputer,
  author  = {Agrawal, Divyansh},
  title   = {{Qwenputer}: a computer compiled into the weights of a pretrained language model},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://github.com/divagr18/qwenputer}
}

title: Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons?
content:
Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons?|
Wed Oct 28 2026
authored by veritas
Preamble
I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others).
At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all?
To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases.
For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another.
Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases.
I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden. As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions.
There were also quite a few I didn't recognize.
Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art.
A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor.
I set out to find my favorite.
A work of art
One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw).
The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents.
I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas.
I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance.
I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative.
The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js.
A peek inside
Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay...
function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply
What?
return {
        summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg",
        result:lethalDosePerKg
}
Huh?
function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage
This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation.
I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts.
Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research.
Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request.
I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked.
Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied!

Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified (BUN_OPTIONS=--preload). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify.
TL;DR
curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js
claude daemon stop --any
BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" claude
To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install.
The problem
Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default.
The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself.
query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after
share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 %
share of all API requests 19.7 %, about 1 in 5 0 %
part of that spend on Opus 96 % —
input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 —
Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate (cost_usd), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %.
The fix (how it works)
no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps setTimeout/setInterval; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary.
Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch. But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once.
Install
Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path.
Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. One of:
# ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc
export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
# ~/.config/fish/config.fish
set -gx BUN_OPTIONS "--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
# ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches
# user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login)
BUN_OPTIONS=--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js
Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another):
#!/bin/sh
HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js
case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in
  *" --preload $HOOK "*) ;;
  *) export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOOK" ;;
esac
: "${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG:=${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/no-agent-summary.log}"
export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG
exec /path/to/the/real/claude "$@"
Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS:
claude daemon stop --any
Env
variable values effect
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off.
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=… on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count.
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line.
Nuances
Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any.
Headless runs need it too: claude -p, cron, CI, editor integrations.
Platform: Linux tested, macOS and Windows untested. On Windows the /$bunfs/ gate most likely never installs the hook.
A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing.
Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment (/proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon.
Verify (after every update)
Preload loads:
BUN_OPTIONS="--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log
Expect preload active mode=off …. No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute.
Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log, run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode.
Fail-open
Matching is by source text: an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen:
the log line or query-source id is renamed;
the callback is passed via fn.bind(...) (no source in toString) or another wrapper;
the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback;
the timer moves to an unwrapped API (timers/promises, a scheduler loop).
So re-run Verify after every update.
Effect
We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero agent_summary requests, and no other side query grew to take its place.
Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped.
Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK task_progress has no summary.
Overhead: one Function.prototype.toString per distinct timer callback, cached in a WeakMap. claude --version: ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement).
Tested versions
Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1, one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file.
version published sha256 static summary forks in a ~2.5-min agent run: no hook / hook pass / hook off notes
2.1.312 2026-10-27 4f4178ce41d8 OK 5 / 5 / 0 latest on 2026-10-28; interactive: 6 no hook, 0 off
2.1.310 2026-10-23 b73676430af1 OK 5 / 5 / 0
2.1.308 2026-10-22 356733f185fa OK 5 / 6 / 0 stable on 2026-10-28; the pass run's agent took 9 steps instead of 8
2.1.301 2026-10-15 bc1aad9982c7 OK 5 / 5 / 0 same with earlier hook builds; interactive off also 0; in daily use since 2026-10-26, 0 agent_summary requests in telemetry
2.1.280 2026-09-22 1e08503dbdf3 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) interactive: -p cannot enable summaries on this version. The agent sat at a permission prompt, so later timers skipped the unchanged transcript
2.1.257 2026-09-01 9a64bda9d872 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) same as 2.1.280
5 / 5 / 0 = the fork happens on this version, merely loading the hook changes nothing, and off removes it.
Why there is no setting for this
The documented switch only turns it on. The SDK option agentProgressSummaries defaults to false, but in the bundle it is one term of an OR, and every code path that writes it sets true. So false changes nothing, and the undocumented CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES can only enable summaries too.
The interval belongs to the server. It comes from a per-model-family server flag and is clamped to 30–240 s. The default is already the minimum, and no value disables the timer.
The obvious env vars miss. DISABLE_NON_ESSENTIAL_MODEL_CALLS, which some packagers set, does not occur in the binary at all. CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 do stop it, but only by taking fork subagents or background agents with it.
The prompt cache makes it cheaper, not cheap. About 98 % of these calls re-read the transcript from cache; the ~2 % that hit a cold cache carry over a third of its cost.
Cost tools that read transcripts don't see it. These requests are not written to the session logs on disk (#104358); only the OpenTelemetry export shows them. The docs section on background token usage doesn't list it either, while Agent View's row summaries are documented as a Haiku-class model refreshing every few minutes.
A cheaper variant already exists, switched off. 2.1.310 ships a short mode: about 2k tokens of notes instead of the full transcript, optionally written by a smaller model. The default is still the full transcript, and only server flags can change it.
Timeline (2026)
version (published) what changed
2.1.32 (Feb 5) the code first appears; dead in public builds
2.1.72 (Mar 9) reachable as an SDK opt-in
2.1.117 (Apr 21) reachable in the interactive CLI behind the fork gate or a server rollout
≤ 2.1.220 (Jul 24) forked skills are always summarized
2.1.232 (Aug 13) on by default for interactive background agents
2.1.300 (Oct 14) interval becomes server-tunable, 30–240 s
2.1.310 (Oct 23) the cheaper short mode lands, switched off
In our telemetry its weekly share of spend went from 3.5–7 % in July (the fork gate was already open for us) to 7.3 % and then 11.8 % in the week we picked up 2.1.233, and to about 16 % by mid-October.

title: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 | Alpine Linux
content:
2026-10-28
GITLAB SECURITY INCIDENT: ATTEMPTED EXPLOITATION OF CVE-2026-97229
On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with.
GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites.
If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org.
WHAT HAPPENED
The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12, but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23, in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9.
The attack: On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out.
Our upgrade didn’t fix the vulnerability: Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch.
If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later.
If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable.
INCIDENT TIMELINE
Date Event
Oct 28 GitLab rebuild complete; all passwords reset and GitLab's secret keys replaced
Oct 27 GitLab closed to everyone except developers and build servers; rebuild started
Oct 26 Found the instance still vulnerable after the upgrade
Oct 25 to 26 Attacker returns and tries to get back in; attempts fail
Oct 24 aports, packages and Oct 21 releases verified against outside records
Oct 23 Attacker's account blocked; Ruby releases the fix
Oct 22 Upgraded to GitLab 19.3.6
Oct 21 Main attack; GitLab crashes, 502 errors and failed CI jobs
Oct 20 Attacker registers an account and starts probing
Oct 13 CVE-2026-97229 published; we upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5 (which had the fix) by mistake
Oct 12 GitLab releases the fix
WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE CAN’T RULE OUT
What we found
Alpine releases and packages were not modified. The October 21 stable releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3), including their ISO images and the minirootfs tarballs the official alpine Docker images are built from, and all packages built from October 20 to 24 came from aports commits we verified against records outside GitLab. See the FAQ below for details.
No signing keys were exposed. The keys that sign Alpine packages and releases are not, and never have been, stored on the GitLab server.
No evidence that the attacker’s code ran: timing probes showed no delays, and we found no unexpected files, keys, hooks or processes.
No private data was returned to the attacker through any web or API request we can see.
Why we can’t be sure
A successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs.
Some logs from the attack day are gone (background job logs, the old container’s filesystem).
We had no logging of outbound network connections, and our hosting provider keeps none either.
What could have been exposed if the attack succeeded
Email addresses, names and IP addresses of all users
Password hashes
2FA secrets, CI/CD variables and runner tokens
Webhook, integration and push mirror credentials
Personal access tokens (stored as hashes)
Private repositories, and confidential issues and merge requests
FAQ
WHY DID WE REBUILD GITLAB IF WE WERE ABLE TO MITIGATE THE ATTACK?
Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch. This removes any foothold a possibly successful exploit could have left behind.
While GitLab is closed, our package mirrors, cgit, and mailing lists/IRC are available as normal.
ARE ALPINE PACKAGES AND RELEASES AFFECTED?
We have found no sign of tampering in aports or the releases.
Every aports commit added October 20 to 22 arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. We checked this against records the attacker could not reach: a developer’s clone and all 45 builders. Every package built from October 20 to 24, on every architecture, came from commits as published on git.alpinelinux.org. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were built from those same verified commits.
We ran these checks on October 24, covering commits from October 20 to 22 and packages built up to October 24. Our GitLab stayed vulnerable until we closed it on October 27, so we are extending the same checks to that date.
IS ALPINE’S RUBY PACKAGE AFFECTED?
The bug is in Ruby’s regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge ship Ruby 3.4.12, and Alpine 3.21 ships Ruby 3.3.13; both include the fix. Run apk upgrade to get it.
WHAT ARE WE CHANGING IN RESPONSE TO THIS EVENT?
Fixed Ruby: the rebuilt instance runs a Ruby with the fix (3.3.13 or later).
Faster patching: apply critical GitLab security releases within a day, and check each release for Ruby or other component patches our own build must apply.
Better logging: record outbound connections from the GitLab host and database connections, and keep logs longer than 14 days.
Signed release tags, so releases can be verified independently of GitLab.

title: A Health Update • furbo.org
content:
A Health Update
I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier.
You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative.
My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope.
Lovely to look at, less lovely to lie on.
Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate. There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back.
It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react.
The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine.
That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do.
Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab.
Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer.
The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite).
Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally.
As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak.
I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again.
I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds over the course of a couple of months and eventually got to the point where I was having five meals a day. Too bad it all tasted bad.
This could also be a graph of my happiness.
One thing that I did to fight my diminished capacity was a daily walk. Anyone who exercises regularly knows that there are always plenty of reasons to avoid it: you didn’t sleep well, you have an important project to finish, or you’re sore from a previous workout. When you’re doing chemo, add feeling like absolute shit to that list.
I still had nerve damage in my spine, so my “walk” was more like a shuffle. Thankfully my wife found some awesome walking sticks to aid with my balance. They are clearly labelled “Not A Medical Device” but they are my most important medical device.
Winter sunsets, exercise, and walking sticks are good medicine.
My daily exercise was just like any gym workout: dread at the start, joy at the end. Sometimes there wasn’t much behind that joy: at my lowest point, a walk around the block on flat ground got my heart rate up to 160 bpm. Breathtaking, literally.
That low point was in March. In the week following my infusion, where I was already feeling like crap, I came down with a type of pneumonia that affects people with weakened immune systems. I had no strength and my blood oxygen level plummeted below 90%. Getting from the living room to the kitchen for a drink of water felt like running a marathon, and then my Apple Watch pinged to inform me that I was having an episode of atrial fibrillation. It was a lot and I honestly had thoughts of “is this how it ends?”
Thankfully, antibiotics battled the pneumonia quickly and the chemo effects subsided. My doctor offered to skip the next cycle of chemotherapy, but I decided to push on. There is only one way to be done with a thing.
Throughout all of the infusions, the nerve damage that occurred before the lymphoma discovery didn’t improve. As I said above, my gait and balance were severely compromised: going up and down stairs was particularly challenging. The tingling sensations on my backside and numbness near my abdomen became a bigger concern with each passing month. It wasn’t getting better and I feared it was a permanent condition.
I finished the last of my infusions in May and my body slowly started to recover. Food started tasting better, and my strength and stamina started to return. My daily walks got longer: first a quarter of a mile, then half a mile, then a mile, and then something fantastic happened.
At the end of a walk around our local state park, I went to grab something in the car glovebox. As I did this, I tilted my head forward and the back of my legs lit up with a feeling I had never felt. Something was changing in my spine: and after a couple of weeks it was clear that this was a sign that the nerves were fixing themselves.
Our guess is that the chemotherapy infusions, which attack white blood cells and other parts of the blood that aid in recovery, had retarded the healing in my nervous system. Now that my body had a chance to repair itself, it was.
I can now go up and down stairs without hanging on for dear life. I’m able to walk without aid, but I still like my walking sticks for longer outings since they let me push myself harder. I’ve also started working out in a gym with a trainer: I told him about my stair issues, and now he has me doing them backwards and by hopping on all fours. I am so happy to look like a doofus, and for the continued improvement I’m seeing with exercise.
My regained ability to walk and a stronger immune system allowed me to leave the house. My first night away from home was a short trip to Topanga Canyon to celebrate an August birthday:
All hail the sunflower goddess!
After that successful trip, we took a short boat ride to have a nice lunch and look at some kelp. It felt so good to be able to do normal things again.
A trip to visit The Blue Forest
One lingering part of my life that hasn’t been reestablished is swimming. All the chemotherapy that has been put into my body has been through a port catheter: a small device under my skin that hooks directly into my carotid artery. Getting an infection there would be a very bad thing, and water increases that risk: be it from ocean water full of living organisms or a swimming pool that kids pee in.
With the current El Niño conditions, that’s been a hard thing: the water is warm and “interesting”. My new gym also has a beautiful Olympic-sized pool for lap swimming. I’m happy to be in this hospital bed doing a final stint of chemotherapy because when I’m done, the port is removed.
This last procedure is to make sure there is no lymphoma in my brain fluids: not a difficult or dangerous treatment and the side effects are minimal. But it does require close monitoring because of the high dosages involved.
In six weeks, I’ll be done and spend the winter in that heated pool so that I can finally swim in my beloved Pacific next summer. The buoys are still there, even though the high surf this summer knocked one out!
Last year was hard, and it got worse over time. This year has also been hard, but it’s gotten better with each passing month. For that I’m grateful.
I’m also grateful for my wife Lauren: it’s impossible to imagine making it through all of this without her help, support, and encouragement. The silver lining in all this strife is that it’s made our relationship much stronger. Thanks sweetie!
As with my previous account, there’s an unwanted coda. No matter how hard I try, there’s a complication at the happy ending!
I had typed up everything above as the doctors and nurses prepared me for the first dose of methotrexate. It takes a while for your blood’s pH level to reach a point where the treatment is safe, so I spent much of the day lying in bed, peeing into urine cups, reminiscing about my year, and typing.
Around 10:30 PM, the medication was in my brain and I was trying to wind down for the night (easier said than done when part of the regimen includes steroids). While scrolling through Tapestry, I noticed quite a few posts about a newly announced PHP vulnerability. This caught my attention because we use it for our blogs, an ad server, delivering Kickstarter rewards, and a bunch of other small things.
(This is the point where family that doesn’t understand what I do for a living continues to not understand what I do for a living.)
It quickly became apparent that this was a big deal and something that could allow an attacker access to our server. I had to shut things down before my brain shut down. Thank goodness the steroids held out.
After a couple of hours, I had blocked access to PHP processes in every nook & cranny of our server. After sending a quick message to our Slack explaining how everything was broken, I collapsed.
The next day started with a head and server that were barely working. Our server was out of LTS, so the first order of business was to get it back onto the latest version of Ubuntu using hospital WiFi. It was a good thing my heart rate and blood pressure were being closely monitored.
(Thank goodness for Lish, which proved to be immune to hospital IT shutting down my ssh connection to accept terms & conditions every few hours. There’s also a “I should have my head examined” joke in here somewhere.)
If you noticed that the Iconfactory sites were kinda broken last week, now you know why. It’s because I was kinda broken last week.
Now I’m finishing this post from a comfy chair on our deck. Typing into the latest version of WordPress and PHP. And I couldn’t be happier.
Written on October 28th, 2026 for Miscellaneous

title: CNC Stone Carving - Carmelite Gothic
content:
CARMELITE MONKS OF WYOMING GOTHIC
GOTHIC
OUR DESIGN
PROGRESS
THE MONKS
CNC STONE CARVING
Home » CNC Stone Carving
CNC Stone Carving
In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place.  However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange.  To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head.
(The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.)
CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks
CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today. 
The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God.
CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk
What is a CNC machine
CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention.
Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process.
CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks
Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings!
CNC lathe and spindle at work carving stone for Carmelite Monks
Prussiani CNC machines
The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs.
The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area.  After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened.  It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night.  At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist.  The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later.
The Carving Process
The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow.  The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver.  He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay.  It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button!  The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space.  And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like. 
The Brother artist carving in mudbox for the Carmelite Monks Gothic
Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers.  The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones.  Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece.  They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone.  At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time.  This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit.  It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come.
Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving.  The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly.  They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves.  They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly.  There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone. 
The Monk Sawyers setting up a table to be Carved for the CNC
The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall.  The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds.  The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter.  This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster.
The monk Wire sawyer puts in plastic shims to support the cut pieces. On the right is the finished product of the wire saw awaiting the denesting of the profiled stones
There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here.  Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here.  The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.

title: Introducing Gemini 4 Carbon
content:
Home
Innovation & AI
