title: We Won’t “Just Hang Out”
content:
What will we do after the Singularity? The standard answer is: “we’ll just hang out”. The infinite vacation, as in the Culture novels. I think this won’t work. “Hanging out” implies:
Other people exist.
They want to hang out with you.
You want to hang out with them.
And the post-scarcity, infinite vacation AI utopia undermines all these assumptions.
Other people exist
The social processes by which people come together and build relationships will disappear. Work, obviously, is pointless in a world of cheap superhuman intelligence. University (really all education beyond teaching people to speak) will be pointless because there’s no work to do and because growing your human capital doesn’t change your life outcomes: you get the same UBI whether you’re illiterate or a PhD.
I met a lot of my friends by writing open-source code, and participating in the community of software engineers. AI is dissolving that community by making human contributions superfluous. If Claude Code has existed when I was starting out, nobody would have cared about Austral or my other open-source projects or my technical blog posts.
As a teenager I tried to install Linux, ran into all kinds of problems, and went on the IRC chatrooms to get help. And in the process I made friends. Today, I would just ask Claude. AI disintermediates everyone, so that we no longer need each other. I still have friends, but I’m running off this pre-AI supply of friends I met through communities of practice. Young people don’t have that privilege.
What even is the point of cities in a world without work? If there’s nothing to do, there is no need to bring people together geographically.
They want to hang out with you
The BATNA to hanging out keeps getting better, cheaper, and more convenient. When people’s sensorium becomes an infinite firehose of AI-generated superstimulus, why would they hang out with anyone?
This is less about AI and more about the trajectory of consumer technology, since many people already live like this: they go to work and watch TikTok. After work, they will just watch TikTok.
You want to hang out with them
As Gregory Conti explains:
[Under] ASI this endless leisure will be passed in diminished, tiresome company, since we will lack the experiences of struggle and striving that generate interesting personalities. Our minds will have atrophied. We will have little of note to say to one another.
The people in the AI utopia will have no skills, no education, no accomplishments. We’ll be lucky if they are even literate. They will not be worth talking to, and you won’t want to hang out with them.
Maybe you and I can hang out with our existing friends. But just iterate this a bit. What about the next generation? How are they going to build meaningful relationships where the social processes that built those relationships are all in the past?
If we get radical life extension, there’s the problem of attrition over the long term: people will drift apart, drop out of society to enter the experience machine, die in accidents, or end their lives out of ennui. So your social network might be a non-renewable resource that gets exhausted over time as your pre-Singularity relationships attrite and can’t be replaced for the reasons above.

title: Getting debug access on a Brother printer over Telnet · Inventor7777
content:
Getting debug access on a Brother printer over Telnet
October 22, 2026
As it turns out, the Brother NC-8700w Command Console is more interesting than it first appears.
Some context
I’ve always enjoyed seeing how things work. It started with hardware and trying to take interesting devices apart, and now I do the same with software. And as I’ve learned how software works, one of the goals I like is accessing hidden features. On Linux based devices, that’s getting a root Linux shell. But what about the printer?
The unsuspecting subject
Is the family Brother MFC-L8900CDW. Unlike the reputations of certain other printer brands and models, this one connects and prints every time. mDNS doesn’t randomly stop working, the paper doesn’t randomly jam, and the toner lasts forever. However, the vendor CLI is limited when it comes to deep system information. (one of these functions is not like the other)
The journey begins
The first step to figuring things out in this day and age is getting a firmware binary and then using AI to attack it from all angles. (Some people are, of course, skilled enough to do this themselves, but I am not one of those people.) On some devices you can straight up download a firmware image, but in Brother’s case, they expect you to use their own downloader. My AI agent first tried just going to the link found in the Brother firmware updater app, but their server rejected a guessed XML request. So after digging a bit deeper into the firmware update tool, we found the list of models and stuff that it accepts. While writing this, I also discovered an interesting tool that might have saved me some reversing trouble had I known about it, but the Brother app had enough info to work it out manually. While Brother could change the format at any time, this is the request that worked for my printer.
curl -sS \
  'https://firmverup.brother.co.jp/kne_bh7_update_nt_ssl/ifax2.asmx/fileUpdate' \
  -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' \
  --data-binary @- <<'XML'
<REQUESTINFO>
  <FIRMUPDATETOOLINFO>
    <FIRMCATEGORY>MAIN</FIRMCATEGORY>
    <OS>MAC</OS>
    <INSPECTMODE>0</INSPECTMODE>
  </FIRMUPDATETOOLINFO>
  <FIRMUPDATEINFO>
    <MODELINFO>
      <NAME>MFC-L8900CDW series</NAME>
      <SPEC>0001</SPEC>
      <DRIVER>EWS</DRIVER>
      <FIRMINFO>
        <FIRM>
          <ID>MAIN</ID>
          <VERSION>ZU2605160228</VERSION>
        </FIRM>
      </FIRMINFO>
    </MODELINFO>
    <DRIVERCNT>1</DRIVERCNT>
    <LOGNO>2</LOGNO>
    <NEEDRESPONSE>1</NEEDRESPONSE>
  </FIRMUPDATEINFO>
</REQUESTINFO>
XML
You can replace the firmware version with B0000000000 instead, and that also works.
In response, Brother’s API returned:
<RESPONSEINFO>
  <FIRMUPDATEINFO>
    <VERSIONCHECK>0</VERSIONCHECK>
    <MEMORYVERSION>a</MEMORYVERSION>
    <FIRMID>MAIN</FIRMID>
    <LATESTVERSION>ZV2608181949</LATESTVERSION>
    <PATH>http://update-akamai.brother.co.jp/CS/D009UD_ZV.djf</PATH>
    <DLTIME>175000</DLTIME>
  </FIRMUPDATEINFO>
</RESPONSEINFO>
Some very descriptive versions, I must say…
The firmware has landed
Now that the firmware was in hand, GPT-6.1 Sol got to work.
Here is what it found, in its own words:
Conclusion
The main application firmware uses the TRON-family T-Kernel real-time
operating system on 32-bit little-endian ARM. Confidence: high. Exact
T-Kernel release, CPU core, and SoC have not been established.
This is positive T-Kernel evidence, not just an absence of Linux strings.

Evidence in extracted/ZlibRo.bin (hex offsets relative to that file)
0x004b0168: T-Kernel/OS SVC in execution
0x019c0450: Software Interrupt (SWI) #6 (T-Kernel/OS & Extended SVC)
0x019c050f: Software Interrupt (SWI) #9 (T-Kernel/DS)
0x019c7d7b: OS_Ver
0x019c7d82: TSysName
0x019c7d8b: T-Kernel
0x019c7d94: TMaxTskId (followed by semaphore/mutex/etc. configuration names)
0x0002a624: TASK STACK INFORMATION for ITRON
0x002b3014: MFC-L8900CDW series (also at 0x00c40f4c and 0x00c4148c)

Evidence in extracted/KernelRo.bin
0x0000e188: T-Monitor Initialize
0x0000e8a5: TM> prompt
0x00009154: Undefined Instruction (ARM)
0x00009170: Undefined Instruction (THUMB)
ARM exception registers R0-R15/CPSR and ARM processor modes are present.
The opening words decode as ARM little-endian instructions, including
SUB lr, lr, #4 (0xe24ee004) and PUSH {r3,r12,lr} (0xe92d5008).
The RTOS kernel is a separate 141,932-byte section loaded at 0x40100000.

Storage and libraries: embedded identification strings, not a security audit
ZlibRo.bin 0x010050e4: Datalight Reliance Nitro v3.0.6 Build 2306EC
ZlibRo.bin 0x003302e4: RTOS Edition for arm; compiled Dec 21 2015
ZlibRo.bin 0x010d6b50: Datalight FlashFX Tera v3.1 Build 2772E
ZlibRo.bin 0x00f391e0: Lua 5.2.3 version identification
ZlibRo.bin 0x008ddaa4: OpenSSL 1.0.1c; other sections identify OpenSSL 1.0.2
ZlibRo.bin 0x005377b8: libpng version 1.6.43
ZlibRo.bin 0x00692ec8: gSOAP/2.7
ZlibRo.bin 0x019bb300: wpa_supplicant v0.5.7-Devicescape
Version labels can survive vendor backports; they do not establish
which vulnerabilities are present or that every bundled module is active.

Flash layout and extraction
The update wrapper starts with PJL EXECUTE BRDOWNLOAD / PROGRAM=FIRM.
This package maps file offset 0x93 to flash address 0xe0060000.
A table of 20-byte labels plus 32-bit little-endian values begins at
package offset 0x8497. It names the kernel, page table, and zlib sections.
The main compressed stream starts at package offset 0x2b2e7, after its
4-byte length. Three streams are stored sequentially. Each stream passed
zlib checksum/end checks and exactly matches the table's expanded size.
The RW source addresses describe their installed flash destinations;
the update package packs those streams immediately after the RO stream.

Output                    Bytes          Load address
PageTable.bin             33,792         0xe0060000
KernelRo.bin             141,932         0x40100000
ZlibRo.bin            28,186,916         0x40222b00
ZlibRw.bin                   700         0x41e00d00
Zlib2Rw.bin            1,526,396         0x43cb8f00

Binwalk found embedded images and other assets in the expanded main
section, but no recognizable Linux filesystem/kernel image. This does
not prove that no separate chip runs other firmware.

Hardware
Brother's model datasheet specifies an 800 MHz main processor, 133 MHz
subprocessor, and 512 MB memory (regional model variations are possible).
The image contains SubCPU/print-engine control messages. This is consistent
with an RTOS application coordinating printing, scanning, UI, networking,
and a separate engine controller. We have not analyzed SUB1 1.35.
Generic CPU vendor names in diagnostic tables do NOT identify the SoC.
The kernel has a T-Monitor debugger/monitor, but that does not establish
that it is accessible through the network telnet port. The firmware also
contains Brother network-configuration telnet commands. A telnet service
is not by itself evidence of a Unix shell.

Sources and comparison material
TRON Forum: T-Kernel and T-Monitor roles
https://www.tron.org/tron-project/what-is-t-kernel/t-kernel/
TRON Forum: official source downloads
https://www.tron.org/source-code-download/
Brother model datasheet (processor/subprocessor/memory)
https://www.brother.lt/-/media/product-downloads/devices/printers/mfc/mfcl8900cdw/mfc-l8900cdw.ashx
STAR Labs: independently inspected a different Brother model using
T-Kernel and similar named/compressed segments. Used as a format lead;
our OS conclusion is based on this package's own extracted evidence.
https://starlabs.sg/blog/2025/11-breaking-into-a-brother-mfc-j1010dw-three-security-flaws-in-a-seemingly-innocent-printer/

...

Configuration records in ZlibRo.bin are 20 bytes each:
  integer value; name pointer; type; count; pointer to own value.
Records for TmConsEnable/TmDebugPort/TmBaudRate have values 0/0/115200.
Kernel code at 0x40109344 reads TmConsEnable and at 0x40109360-0x40109368
skips initial serial-console initialization when that value is zero.
These are compiled defaults, not measurements of current RAM settings.
Separate application records ConsDrvEnable=1 and DEBUGPORT=2 exist;
these names alone do not establish UART pin numbers or a remote route.

T-Monitor character I/O accesses memory-mapped hardware at 0xd0c00000:
  0x4010e058: output character routine
  0x4010e0d0: serial initialization, writes T-Monitor Initialize
  0x4010e1a0: input character routine
  0x4010e7c4 and 0x4010e8c0: interactive loops with TM> prompt
Input/output can lazily initialize the serial block even when initial
console initialization was skipped, so TmConsEnable=0 does not prove
that later monitor entry is impossible.

At 0x4010e280 the command dispatcher loads table address 0x41e00e18.
It walks 12-byte records (name, alias, handler), stopping at a null name.
The initial table is in extracted/ZlibRw.bin at offset 0x118:
  Help, H, handler 0x4010e318
  null, null, handler 0x4010e1f8
The terminator's handler prints Unsupported command. No full memory,
register, breakpoint, or step-command suite is present in this initial
table. This narrows the generic T-Monitor description from earlier.

Separate Brother debug console
The application contains telnetddebug and /telnetdebug_q identifiers,
Enter debug user mode text, and help strings for debug symbols, task
stacks, heap usage, uptime, and console output redirection. Their presence
is a lead; it does not establish successful access or T-Monitor bridging.
If you skipped past that, I can’t blame you. It could be interesting to some folks, though, which is why I included it.
Printer’s tech stack
The printer runs T-Kernel, a TRON-family real-time OS.
Component Info
CPU architecture 32-bit ARM, little-endian
Storage filesystem Datalight Reliance Nitro 3.0.6
Flash management Datalight FlashFX Tera 3.1
Scripting Lua 5.2.3
Other libraries OpenSSL, gSOAP, libpng, wpa_supplicant
Firmware structure Separate kernel, compressed application code, embedded web/UI assets
Brother specifies an 800 MHz main processor, 133 MHz subprocessor, and 512 MB RAM. The firmware contains messages for communicating with that subprocessor and controlling the print engine. Brother datasheet
The interesting part: getting debug access without modifying anything
This is probably the part you came for!
If you have telnet enabled on your printer (easy to enable via the web UI), it is very easy to access the three debugging modes.
Use these at your own risk! You can seriously mess up the system if you modify the parameters incorrectly.
Log into the command console using your admin password and just hit enter when it asks for username. Once you’re at the Local> prompt, simply type SET USER 640184.571119
inventor7777@Mac-Studio - 20:17 ~ % telnet 192.168.50.16
Trying 192.168.50.16...
Connected to 192.168.50.16.
Escape character is '^]'.

Welcome. Type <return>, enter password at # prompt

# 
Brother NC-8700w Command Console
 Copyright(C) 2000-2017 Brother Industries, Ltd.
 KASAGO TCP/IP Copyright (c) 2011 ZUKEN ELMIC, Inc.

 Interface 1 : NC-9200h, Ethernet 10/100/1000BASE-T      (Inactive)
 Interface 2 : NC-8700w, IEEE 802.11b/g/n                  (Active)
 Interface 2 is selected for configuration

 Type HELP for command list



Enter username> 
Local> SET USER 640184.571119

Enter debug user mode.

Local> HELP

EXIT/^D                  Exit program
HElp                     Information on available commands
INitialize               Reset unit
CLear                    Remove configuration item
SET                      Modify unit parameters
SHow                     Display unit parameters
ZEro                     Zero statistical counts
DEbug                                Execute debug functions
REDirect                             Redirect printf() output
WATch [<addr>[ <intvl/cond>[ <unit>]]] Watch memory function
SNTPDEBUG                SNTP for debug functions

Type 'HElp <cmd>' for more information
The firmware also contains wireless QA and wireless development access modes, which I haven’t looked deeply into. Wireless QA is accessible via SET USER 031227, and wireless development is available via SET USER 031227.040119
I haven’t played around with the debug console (or the CLI in general, for that matter) very much, but the firmware reveals a TON of commands. Instead of making this post crazy long, my AI compiled this HTML of every command available. I haven’t tested them all, so take it with a grain of salt, but GPT-6.1 Sol is actually pretty smart!
Again, I did not extensively test any of these commands as I prefer to have a working printer, but it’s pretty interesting. I did check the heap using DEBUG SHOW HEAP, and it really does give a full list of all running tasks and how much heap they use. Neat!
If this post didn’t satisfy your hunger for Brother printer reverse engineering, another interesting read is this Star Labs Brother investigation, where they dive a bit deeper into how these printers actually work.

title: A faster way to compute signed 64-bit floor division by constants
content:
Ben Joffe

See also, other optimisation articles:
Faster day-of-week functions
Faster time-of-day functions
A faster way to compute signed 64-bit floor division by constants
The missing chapter of Hacker's Delight
27 October 2026
What is signed integer floor division?
Signed integer floor division is where you do a/b and get a result that rounds towards −∞,
whereas standard (“truncated”) signed division rounds towards 0.
As stated in Hacker's Delight: “[I suspect that] floor division more often gives the result you want”.
This article is about full-range floor division where the divisor is known at compile time.
Despite the usefulness of this function, the world of integer floor division is in shambles:
Mainstream compilers and many languages do not provide it natively (eg. C/C++/Go/Swift).
Languages and software libraries that do implement it seem to almost never use the fastest algorithms.
At least one highly prominent software library had a buggy overflowing implementation for over 4 years! (detailed later)
Typical online searches and LLM prompts usually only surface the slow algorithms
And finally, Hacker's Delight (basically the bible on low-level computer math), has almost nothing to say about it!
This blog post aims to not only shine light on the fast algorithms, but will also introduce a new fast approach which, with ideal compilation:
On ARM, benches 10–20% faster throughput than existing algorithms for most 64-bit divisors (occasionally tied), with equal or better latency
On x86, benches:
~5-10% faster throughput for around 80% of positive 64-bit divisors (60% of negative divisors)
slower in the remaining x86 cases, and usually worse (but competitive) latency
The benchmark section has a detailed overview showing per-divisor results over many platforms, for throughput and latency.
It works in all bit-widths, and may find use on some 32-bit or SIMD applications, but the biggest benefit is in 64-bit.
It also can be used for faster positive-modulus, and faster "Euclidean" division (differs to floor division for negative divisors).
Floor division can be much faster than you probably realise.
Below is a snapshot throughput benchmark for division by 86400 (the number of seconds in one day), the kind of performance you can expect using most languages' built-in methods, vs fast alternatives outlined in this blog.
Note: in the bar chart: lower = faster.

and Snapdragon X1-26-100

*Rust provides "div_euclid", which matches floor-div for positive divisors.
See the benchmark section for a deeper comparison across over 40 divisors.
Since some people visiting this page will be just looking to copy/paste code, I'll start with this function builder on the right:
Using this form, you can choose any bit-width and any divisor to get a copy/paste function ready to go.
There is also reference algorithm (a reusable C++ template with additional microarchitectural performance tweaks).
As you can see, the technique is so simple that I'd expect that somebody has done this before, but I've looked around and not found it documented anywhere. If it turns out to have been done before, at least this page will make it discoverable.
For the rest of us, I'll cover a narrative about floor division, which matches my process of discovery... And if you want to create a fast library or compiler/language implementation, this will be your one-stop shop.
If you want to skip the history lesson, you can jump straight to the new stuff.

Which Algorithm Should I Use?
Annexure A. Proof
New Fast Division Functions:
Bit-Width:
64-bit
32-bit
16-bit
8-bit

Divisor:
−
+
// MIT License Click to show
// Fast floor division by 86400.
// (rounds towards negative infinity).
// Accurate over the full signed 64-bit range.
// Sign-selected multiplier variant.
// Optional ref:
// https://www.benjoffe.com/fast-floordiv#fn=i64_86400
inline int64_t fast_i64_floordiv_86400(int64_t x) {
  const int64_t M = ((__int128(1) << 79) / 86400 + 1);
  const int64_t m = M + (x >> 63);
  return (__int128) x * m >> 79;
}
For the avoidance of doubt, the license only applies if you copy/paste the comment and code verbatim. No license is required if you re-write the same logic in your code.
Testing
A set of 65535 divisors from -32768 to 32767 for 64-bit can be generated into a single self-contained C++ file. It includes a boundary test in the same file.
See the comment at the top of the download for how to build and run it.
⬇ Download 64-bit Functions + Test
STARTING WITH TRUNCATED (STANDARD) DIVISION
DEEP LINK
Let's suppose you want to convert a Unix timestamp measured in seconds, to rata-die (a day count). And let's also suppose you forgot how to do this properly, and you use standard ("truncated") division.
We need to divide by 86400 (60×60×24). We'll use a 64-bit timestamp, since a 32-bit timestamp can only hold about ±68 years.
You'll be very happy with this implementation on the right until somebody hands you a timestamp before 1970!
C++ Standard Division (not floor-div)
Given: x — signed 64-bit integer
const int64_t rd = x / 86400;
return rd;
The above function returns incorrect results for most negative values.
Of course, you should be using floor division, the type of division that's useful for tracking repeating patterns like timestamps, angle rotations, tile positions etc. This is the type of division where the associated "%" operation is a proper positive modulus, not that fake modulus that "%" provides in C++, JavaScript etc.
Nonetheless, it's useful to understand what is going on under the hood when doing standard division like this. The pseudocode to the right shows what the compiled assembly is actually doing. It's essentially a mul‑shift and bump-by-1 for negatives.
Standard Division Compiled Steps (pseudocode)
const i64 M = (i128(1) << 77) / 86400 + 1 // Precomputed
const i128 wide = i128(x) * M
const i64  tbit = wide >> 77      // high64(wide) >> 13
const i64  sign = u64(x) >> 63   // ts < 0 ? 1 : 0
return tbit + sign
x86-64 Latency Steps
Step Computation 1 Computation 2
1 wide = ts * M
2 mul-latency sign = u64(ts) >> 63
3 mul-latency
4 high64bits(wide) >> 13
5 ... + sign
If you haven't bit twiddled much, the step u64(ts) >> 63 might seem odd. This is just moving the highest-bit down to the bottom. Since the top bit is the sign-bit on 2's complement computers, this leaves a 1 for negative numbers and a 0 for positive numbers.
Aside on Uncooperative Divisors
Deep link
Btw, if you're new to all this, you might think: "Great! I now understand how signed division works at the compiler level!"
Sorry to burst the bubble, but here's what the same thing looks like for 64-bit division by 100:
Divide by 100 (C++)
Given: x — signed 64-bit integer
return x / 100;
Divide by 100 low level steps (pseudocode)
Given: x — signed 64-bit integer
const i64 M = (i128(1) << 70) / 100 + 1
const i128 wide = i128(x) * M
const i64 tbit = ((wide >> 64) + x) >> 6
const i64 sign = u64(x) >> 63
return tbit + sign
You should notice we now have some extra junk in there: ((wide >> 64) + x) >> 6.
This is required because the magic multiplier for 100 happens to require all 64-bits for M.
This causes the top bit to be 1, making M a negative number, and as computed, the value of M ends up2^64 lower than it should be. Since we compute x * M, the value of wide is thus 2^64 * x lower than it should be. By adding x to the upper-register of the wide double-register result, we correct for it perfectly.
Divisors that require these corrections are referred to by some authors as uncooperative divisors.
x86-64 Latency Steps
Step Computation 1 Computation 2
1 wide = x * M
2 mul-latency sign = u64(x) >> 63
3 mul-latency
4 high64bits(wide) + x
5 ... >> 6
6 ... + sign
The main takeaway here is that regular division is usually the cost of around 1 multiplication + 2-3 cycles.
FIXING THE BUG
DEEP LINK
Okay, back to div 86400; you get bitten by the bug, and decide to patch it. It's pretty clear that the bug can occur when x < 0, but not always. If it's negative and divisible by 86400, it still works.
So therefore, it needs adjusting when rem < 0, like so:
But you think to yourself, surely there must be a faster way? Computing the modulus is almost as expensive as the division itself, and it gets thrown away after the bump in our theoretical use-case.
The 2nd example to the right is perhaps the first simplification that may come to mind, but it's actually slower! You can visit the Godbolt link to see that it produces more assembly lines...
C++
const int64_t div = x / 86400;
const int64_t rem = x % 86400;
return div - (rem < 0);
C++ (attractive, but slower)
Godbolt (this and above) 
const int64_t div = x / 86400;
return div - (div * 86400 > x);
Okay, screw this unintuitive nonsense, let's Google "fast floor division in c++", and get an AI summary like this (cached PDF export).
This AI summary is very misleading, as it falsely claims "Here are the fastest, branchless methods for each scenario.", before presenting a constant floor division routine that is no better than our attempt here, despite faster ways being known for 30 years+ (although it handles negative divisors at least).
In any case, the code to the right is what it suggests.
At least now we can have a flexible utility function, and it seems GCC and Clang can compile this into the same assembly as our previous version when the divisor is hard-coded (see on Godbolt ).
This is basically the same function used by Java Math.floorDiv , Python's numpy , Zig , Ruby and many other libraries.
Common Solution for signed divisors
Given: x, y — Signed Integers Compute x FLOOR_DIV y
const int64_t div = x / y;
const int64_t rem = x % y;
return div - (rem != 0 && (x ^ y) < 0);
WHAT HACKER'S DELIGHT HAS TO SAY ABOUT IT
DEEP LINK
Hacker's Delight, 2nd Edition, has a section listed in the table of contents: "10–12 Applicability to Modulus and Floor Division". That sounds promising!
It comes immediately after dozens of awesome pages with fancy tricks for other types of division (signed, unsigned etc.).
The entire contents of Section 10–12:
“ It might seem that turning modulus or floor division by a constant into multiplication would be simpler, in that the “add 1 if the dividend is negative” step could be omitted. This is not the case. The methods given above do not apply in any obvious way to modulus and floor division. Perhaps something could be worked out; it might involve altering the multiplier m slightly, depending upon the sign of the dividend. ”
— Henry S. Warren, Jr.,   Hacker's Delight, 2nd Edition
That's the whole section...
Normally, it might be copyright infringement to duplicate an entire section from a book, but in this case it's so short I think I'm covered by fair use.
Although Warren doesn't offer any solutions, the section highlighted in yellow perfectly predicts the new approach I'll introduce later.
FASTER TECHNIQUES
DEEP LINK
At this point, you would be forgiven in thinking this can't be optimised any further; maybe it can't for runtime divisors (I have not investigated, since I've focused mainly on compile-time). Looking further, the first Google Search result: the archaeological remains of the once bustling Stack Overflow. The title looks promising: Fast floor of a signed integer division in C / C++ .
The post is from 2017, and has 6 answers. The OP and the top five up-voted results all use variations of the above technique.
Finally, if you scroll to the bottom, you see after seven years, user ufoguy finally posts an answer that is notably faster for compile-time divisors:
"[Not] sure why this one wasn't mentioned; just one division, no modulo, branch-less:"
C++ - Floor division (where b > 0)
int floor_div(int a, int b) {
    return (a + (a < 0)) / b - (a < 0);
}
By my benchmarks this gives a neat improvement, it runs around 50% greater throughput on most devices.
What does ufoguy get for adding this?
No thanks, no up-vote, just a comment pointing out that this does not account for negative divisors.
A fair caveat. If we're going to make a fast general purpose lib, it might as well be flexible.
Luckily, the general case was solved at least as far back as the 90s.
It is documented clearly on page 6 of Division by Invariant Integers using Multiplication - Granlund, Montgomery, 1994.
Using the technique from that paper, we can create a simple flexible template function (non-zero divisor known at compile time).
I've prepared an example using that technique which can be called like this in C++: floor_div<int64_t(86400)>(timestamp);.
Note that the paper demonstrates a fully branchless version, but I prefer the one above for division by constants, as it's just blindly clear what's going on, and also given the branch is compile-time, it's guaranteed to simplify. Compilers readily recognise the repeated comparison eg. (x < 0) and reuse the result. However see a Godbolt comparison of the fully branchless version to see how MSVC struggles to simplify it.
Seems like floor-div is solved right?
We're only just getting started...
C++ Granlund Montgomery floor div (v1)
#include <type_traits>
template <auto D>
constexpr decltype(D) floor_div(decltype(D) x) {
    static_assert(std::is_integral_v<decltype(D)> &&
        std::is_signed_v<decltype(D)> && D != 0,
        "divisor must be a signed non-zero integer");
    if constexpr (D > 0)
        return (x + (x < 0)) / D - (x < 0);
    else
        return (x - (x > 0)) / D - (x > 0);
}
Code highlighted in green is compile-time only and has no runtime impact.
THE POSITIVE DIVISOR XOR TRICK
DEEP LINK
The division in the previous section was, at best, a mul-shift plus 5-6 cycles.
Why so many?
One for x < 0 (or x > 0).
One to add that to the numerator.
One to subtract that from the result.
Two or three for the division itself (remember earlier we showed division is a mul-shift + 2-3 cycles?)
Luckily for us, Granlund and Montgomery have another trick up their sleeve, but it's only specified for positive divisors:
Floor Div - Positive Fast Path (v1)
Given: D — Positive 64-bit integer
Pre-Solve: M — Magic-multiplier
Pre-Solve: S — Magic-shift
i64 s = x >> 63 // x < 0 ? -1 : 0
u64 a = x ^ s
u64 b = (u128) a * M >> S
i64 c = b ^ s
return c;
The diagram to the right is my attempt at visualising this.
It's a bit crazy!

title: A Health Update • furbo.org
content:
A Health Update
I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier.
You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative.
My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope.
Lovely to look at, less lovely to lie on.
Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate. There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back.
It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react.
The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine.
That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do.
Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab.
Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer.
The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite).
Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally.
As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak.
I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again.
I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds over the course of a couple of months and eventually got to the point where I was having five meals a day. Too bad it all tasted bad.
This could also be a graph of my happiness.
One thing that I did to fight my diminished capacity was a daily walk. Anyone who exercises regularly knows that there are always plenty of reasons to avoid it: you didn’t sleep well, you have an important project to finish, or you’re sore from a previous workout. When you’re doing chemo, add feeling like absolute shit to that list.
I still had nerve damage in my spine, so my “walk” was more like a shuffle. Thankfully my wife found some awesome walking sticks to aid with my balance. They are clearly labelled “Not A Medical Device” but they are my most important medical device.
Winter sunsets, exercise, and walking sticks are good medicine.
My daily exercise was just like any gym workout: dread at the start, joy at the end. Sometimes there wasn’t much behind that joy: at my lowest point, a walk around the block on flat ground got my heart rate up to 160 bpm. Breathtaking, literally.
That low point was in March. In the week following my infusion, where I was already feeling like crap, I came down with a type of pneumonia that affects people with weakened immune systems. I had no strength and my blood oxygen level plummeted below 90%. Getting from the living room to the kitchen for a drink of water felt like running a marathon, and then my Apple Watch pinged to inform me that I was having an episode of atrial fibrillation. It was a lot and I honestly had thoughts of “is this how it ends?”
Thankfully, antibiotics battled the pneumonia quickly and the chemo effects subsided. My doctor offered to skip the next cycle of chemotherapy, but I decided to push on. There is only one way to be done with a thing.
Throughout all of the infusions, the nerve damage that occurred before the lymphoma discovery didn’t improve. As I said above, my gait and balance were severely compromised: going up and down stairs was particularly challenging. The tingling sensations on my backside and numbness near my abdomen became a bigger concern with each passing month. It wasn’t getting better and I feared it was a permanent condition.
I finished the last of my infusions in May and my body slowly started to recover. Food started tasting better, and my strength and stamina started to return. My daily walks got longer: first a quarter of a mile, then half a mile, then a mile, and then something fantastic happened.
At the end of a walk around our local state park, I went to grab something in the car glovebox. As I did this, I tilted my head forward and the back of my legs lit up with a feeling I had never felt. Something was changing in my spine: and after a couple of weeks it was clear that this was a sign that the nerves were fixing themselves.
Our guess is that the chemotherapy infusions, which attack white blood cells and other parts of the blood that aid in recovery, had retarded the healing in my nervous system. Now that my body had a chance to repair itself, it was.
I can now go up and down stairs without hanging on for dear life. I’m able to walk without aid, but I still like my walking sticks for longer outings since they let me push myself harder. I’ve also started working out in a gym with a trainer: I told him about my stair issues, and now he has me doing them backwards and by hopping on all fours. I am so happy to look like a doofus, and for the continued improvement I’m seeing with exercise.
My regained ability to walk and a stronger immune system allowed me to leave the house. My first night away from home was a short trip to Topanga Canyon to celebrate an August birthday:
All hail the sunflower goddess!
After that successful trip, we took a short boat ride to have a nice lunch and look at some kelp. It felt so good to be able to do normal things again.
A trip to visit The Blue Forest
One lingering part of my life that hasn’t been reestablished is swimming. All the chemotherapy that has been put into my body has been through a port catheter: a small device under my skin that hooks directly into my carotid artery. Getting an infection there would be a very bad thing, and water increases that risk: be it from ocean water full of living organisms or a swimming pool that kids pee in.
With the current El Niño conditions, that’s been a hard thing: the water is warm and “interesting”. My new gym also has a beautiful Olympic-sized pool for lap swimming. I’m happy to be in this hospital bed doing a final stint of chemotherapy because when I’m done, the port is removed.
This last procedure is to make sure there is no lymphoma in my brain fluids: not a difficult or dangerous treatment and the side effects are minimal. But it does require close monitoring because of the high dosages involved.
In six weeks, I’ll be done and spend the winter in that heated pool so that I can finally swim in my beloved Pacific next summer. The buoys are still there, even though the high surf this summer knocked one out!
Last year was hard, and it got worse over time. This year has also been hard, but it’s gotten better with each passing month. For that I’m grateful.
I’m also grateful for my wife Lauren: it’s impossible to imagine making it through all of this without her help, support, and encouragement. The silver lining in all this strife is that it’s made our relationship much stronger. Thanks sweetie!
As with my previous account, there’s an unwanted coda. No matter how hard I try, there’s a complication at the happy ending!
I had typed up everything above as the doctors and nurses prepared me for the first dose of methotrexate. It takes a while for your blood’s pH level to reach a point where the treatment is safe, so I spent much of the day lying in bed, peeing into urine cups, reminiscing about my year, and typing.
Around 10:30 PM, the medication was in my brain and I was trying to wind down for the night (easier said than done when part of the regimen includes steroids). While scrolling through Tapestry, I noticed quite a few posts about a newly announced PHP vulnerability. This caught my attention because we use it for our blogs, an ad server, delivering Kickstarter rewards, and a bunch of other small things.
(This is the point where family that doesn’t understand what I do for a living continues to not understand what I do for a living.)
It quickly became apparent that this was a big deal and something that could allow an attacker access to our server. I had to shut things down before my brain shut down. Thank goodness the steroids held out.
After a couple of hours, I had blocked access to PHP processes in every nook & cranny of our server. After sending a quick message to our Slack explaining how everything was broken, I collapsed.
The next day started with a head and server that were barely working. Our server was out of LTS, so the first order of business was to get it back onto the latest version of Ubuntu using hospital WiFi. It was a good thing my heart rate and blood pressure were being closely monitored.
(Thank goodness for Lish, which proved to be immune to hospital IT shutting down my ssh connection to accept terms & conditions every few hours. There’s also a “I should have my head examined” joke in here somewhere.)
If you noticed that the Iconfactory sites were kinda broken last week, now you know why. It’s because I was kinda broken last week.
Now I’m finishing this post from a comfy chair on our deck. Typing into the latest version of WordPress and PHP. And I couldn’t be happier.
Written on October 28th, 2026 for Miscellaneous

title: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 | Alpine Linux
content:
2026-10-28
GITLAB SECURITY INCIDENT: ATTEMPTED EXPLOITATION OF CVE-2026-97229
On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with.
GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites.
If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org.
WHAT HAPPENED
The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12, but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23, in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9.
The attack: On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out.
Our upgrade didn’t fix the vulnerability: Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch.
If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later.
If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable.
INCIDENT TIMELINE
Date Event
Oct 28 GitLab rebuild complete; all passwords reset and GitLab's secret keys replaced
Oct 27 GitLab closed to everyone except developers and build servers; rebuild started
Oct 26 Found the instance still vulnerable after the upgrade
Oct 25 to 26 Attacker returns and tries to get back in; attempts fail
Oct 24 aports, packages and Oct 21 releases verified against outside records
Oct 23 Attacker's account blocked; Ruby releases the fix
Oct 22 Upgraded to GitLab 19.3.6
Oct 21 Main attack; GitLab crashes, 502 errors and failed CI jobs
Oct 20 Attacker registers an account and starts probing
Oct 13 CVE-2026-97229 published; we upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5 (which had the fix) by mistake
Oct 12 GitLab releases the fix
WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE CAN’T RULE OUT
What we found
Alpine releases and packages were not modified. The October 21 stable releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3), including their ISO images and the minirootfs tarballs the official alpine Docker images are built from, and all packages built from October 20 to 24 came from aports commits we verified against records outside GitLab. See the FAQ below for details.
No signing keys were exposed. The keys that sign Alpine packages and releases are not, and never have been, stored on the GitLab server.
No evidence that the attacker’s code ran: timing probes showed no delays, and we found no unexpected files, keys, hooks or processes.
No private data was returned to the attacker through any web or API request we can see.
Why we can’t be sure
A successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs.
Some logs from the attack day are gone (background job logs, the old container’s filesystem).
We had no logging of outbound network connections, and our hosting provider keeps none either.
What could have been exposed if the attack succeeded
Email addresses, names and IP addresses of all users
Password hashes
2FA secrets, CI/CD variables and runner tokens
Webhook, integration and push mirror credentials
Personal access tokens (stored as hashes)
Private repositories, and confidential issues and merge requests
FAQ
WHY DID WE REBUILD GITLAB IF WE WERE ABLE TO MITIGATE THE ATTACK?
Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch. This removes any foothold a possibly successful exploit could have left behind.
While GitLab is closed, our package mirrors, cgit, and mailing lists/IRC are available as normal.
ARE ALPINE PACKAGES AND RELEASES AFFECTED?
We have found no sign of tampering in aports or the releases.
Every aports commit added October 20 to 22 arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. We checked this against records the attacker could not reach: a developer’s clone and all 45 builders. Every package built from October 20 to 24, on every architecture, came from commits as published on git.alpinelinux.org. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were built from those same verified commits.
We ran these checks on October 24, covering commits from October 20 to 22 and packages built up to October 24. Our GitLab stayed vulnerable until we closed it on October 27, so we are extending the same checks to that date.
IS ALPINE’S RUBY PACKAGE AFFECTED?
The bug is in Ruby’s regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge ship Ruby 3.4.12, and Alpine 3.21 ships Ruby 3.3.13; both include the fix. Run apk upgrade to get it.
WHAT ARE WE CHANGING IN RESPONSE TO THIS EVENT?
Fixed Ruby: the rebuilt instance runs a Ruby with the fix (3.3.13 or later).
Faster patching: apply critical GitLab security releases within a day, and check each release for Ruby or other component patches our own build must apply.
Better logging: record outbound connections from the GitLab host and database connections, and keep logs longer than 14 days.
Signed release tags, so releases can be verified independently of GitLab.

title: Claude Code burns ~15-20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line: a Bun preload that turns agent_summary off · by Flamerix AI, flamerix.ai · MIT · GitHub
content:
Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off
by Flamerix AI · MIT License
Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified (BUN_OPTIONS=--preload). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify.
TL;DR
curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js
claude daemon stop --any
BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" claude
To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install.
The problem
Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default.
The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself.
query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after
share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 %
share of all API requests 19.7 %, about 1 in 5 0 %
part of that spend on Opus 96 % —
input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 —
Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate (cost_usd), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %.
The fix (how it works)
no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps setTimeout/setInterval; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary.
Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch. But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once.
Install
Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path.
Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. One of:
# ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc
export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
# ~/.config/fish/config.fish
set -gx BUN_OPTIONS "--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
# ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches
# user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login)
BUN_OPTIONS=--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js
Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another):
#!/bin/sh
HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js
case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in
  *" --preload $HOOK "*) ;;
  *) export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOOK" ;;
esac
: "${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG:=${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/no-agent-summary.log}"
export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG
exec /path/to/the/real/claude "$@"
Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS:
claude daemon stop --any
Env
variable values effect
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off.
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=… on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count.
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line.
Nuances
Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any.
Headless runs need it too: claude -p, cron, CI, editor integrations.
Platform: Linux tested, macOS and Windows untested. On Windows the /$bunfs/ gate most likely never installs the hook.
A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing.
Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment (/proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon.
Verify (after every update)
Preload loads:
BUN_OPTIONS="--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log
Expect preload active mode=off …. No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute.
Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log, run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode.
Fail-open
Matching is by source text: an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen:
the log line or query-source id is renamed;
the callback is passed via fn.bind(...) (no source in toString) or another wrapper;
the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback;
the timer moves to an unwrapped API (timers/promises, a scheduler loop).
So re-run Verify after every update.
Effect
We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero agent_summary requests, and no other side query grew to take its place.
Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped.
Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK task_progress has no summary.
Overhead: one Function.prototype.toString per distinct timer callback, cached in a WeakMap. claude --version: ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement).
Tested versions
Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1, one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file.
version published sha256 static summary forks in a ~2.5-min agent run: no hook / hook pass / hook off notes
2.1.312 2026-10-27 4f4178ce41d8 OK 5 / 5 / 0 latest on 2026-10-28; interactive: 6 no hook, 0 off
2.1.310 2026-10-23 b73676430af1 OK 5 / 5 / 0
2.1.308 2026-10-22 356733f185fa OK 5 / 6 / 0 stable on 2026-10-28; the pass run's agent took 9 steps instead of 8
2.1.301 2026-10-15 bc1aad9982c7 OK 5 / 5 / 0 same with earlier hook builds; interactive off also 0; in daily use since 2026-10-26, 0 agent_summary requests in telemetry
2.1.280 2026-09-22 1e08503dbdf3 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) interactive: -p cannot enable summaries on this version. The agent sat at a permission prompt, so later timers skipped the unchanged transcript
2.1.257 2026-09-01 9a64bda9d872 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) same as 2.1.280
5 / 5 / 0 = the fork happens on this version, merely loading the hook changes nothing, and off removes it.
Why there is no setting for this
The documented switch only turns it on. The SDK option agentProgressSummaries defaults to false, but in the bundle it is one term of an OR, and every code path that writes it sets true. So false changes nothing, and the undocumented CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES can only enable summaries too.
The interval belongs to the server. It comes from a per-model-family server flag and is clamped to 30–240 s. The default is already the minimum, and no value disables the timer.
The obvious env vars miss. DISABLE_NON_ESSENTIAL_MODEL_CALLS, which some packagers set, does not occur in the binary at all. CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 do stop it, but only by taking fork subagents or background agents with it.
The prompt cache makes it cheaper, not cheap. About 98 % of these calls re-read the transcript from cache; the ~2 % that hit a cold cache carry over a third of its cost.
Cost tools that read transcripts don't see it. These requests are not written to the session logs on disk (#104358); only the OpenTelemetry export shows them. The docs section on background token usage doesn't list it either, while Agent View's row summaries are documented as a Haiku-class model refreshing every few minutes.
A cheaper variant already exists, switched off. 2.1.310 ships a short mode: about 2k tokens of notes instead of the full transcript, optionally written by a smaller model. The default is still the full transcript, and only server flags can change it.
Timeline (2026)
version (published) what changed
2.1.32 (Feb 5) the code first appears; dead in public builds
2.1.72 (Mar 9) reachable as an SDK opt-in
2.1.117 (Apr 21) reachable in the interactive CLI behind the fork gate or a server rollout
≤ 2.1.220 (Jul 24) forked skills are always summarized
2.1.232 (Aug 13) on by default for interactive background agents
2.1.300 (Oct 14) interval becomes server-tunable, 30–240 s
2.1.310 (Oct 23) the cheaper short mode lands, switched off
In our telemetry its weekly share of spend went from 3.5–7 % in July (the fork gate was already open for us) to 7.3 % and then 11.8 % in the week we picked up 2.1.233, and to about 16 % by mid-October.

title: CNC Stone Carving - Carmelite Gothic
content:
CARMELITE MONKS OF WYOMING GOTHIC
GOTHIC
OUR DESIGN
PROGRESS
THE MONKS
CNC STONE CARVING
Home » CNC Stone Carving
CNC Stone Carving
In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place.  However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange.  To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head.
(The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.)
CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks
CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today. 
The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God.
CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk
What is a CNC machine
CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention.
Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process.
CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks
Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings!
CNC lathe and spindle at work carving stone for Carmelite Monks
Prussiani CNC machines
The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs.
The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area.  After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened.  It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night.  At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist.  The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later.
The Carving Process
The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow.  The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver.  He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay.  It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button!  The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space.  And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like. 
The Brother artist carving in mudbox for the Carmelite Monks Gothic
Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers.  The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones.  Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece.  They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone.  At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time.  This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit.  It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come.
Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving.  The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly.  They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves.  They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly.  There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone. 
The Monk Sawyers setting up a table to be Carved for the CNC
The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall.  The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds.  The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter.  This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster.
The monk Wire sawyer puts in plastic shims to support the cut pieces. On the right is the finished product of the wire saw awaiting the denesting of the profiled stones
There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here.  Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here.  The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.

title: SMS of Death: zero-click Android telephony DoS
content:
SMS OF DEATH
Vulnerability
Impact
Why it matters
Timeline
PoC
ANDROID TELEPHONY · ZERO-CLICK · REMOTE DOS
SMS of Death
A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls (including emergency calls), with zero interaction from the victim.
Download APK
Source
Google Issue Tracker
⚠ Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading.
COMPONENT
WapPushOverSms
frameworks/opt/telephony
INTERACTION
None
zero-click, silent
VECTOR
Remote SMS
WAP Push, port 2948
VENDOR STATUS
● Won't Fix
classified Non-Security
REPORTER
Mark Blaszczyk
independent
REPORTED
5 May 2026
Android & Devices VRP
DISCLOSED
29 Oct 2026
after 90-day timeline
CVE
None
no CVE issued
01 / The vulnerability
An unchecked cast turns a 5-byte header into a negative array size
When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar. The value comes back as a long, is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array:
// WapPushOverSms.java:217  header length read as long, cast with no bounds check
int headerLength = (int) pduDecoder.getValue32();
    ...
// WapPushOverSms.java:244  the cast value is used as an array size
byte[] header = new byte[headerLength];
A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000. Cast to a signed 32-bit int, that is -2147483648. Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone:
E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main
E AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone
E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169)
E AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627)
The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number.
02 / Impact
Remote, silent, and recoverable only with effort
Zero-click. The victim does nothing. No tap, no open, no notification.
Silent. Nothing appears in Messages; the attacker's number is never shown.
Calls drop, including emergency calls. Active voice calls terminate with DisconnectCause CS_DEATH as the process restarts.
Telephony blackout. 1-2 seconds of no service per message while com.android.phone restarts.
Carrier redelivery amplifies it. Unacknowledged messages are re-sent by the carrier, re-crashing the phone; a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing.
~20 messages render the device unusable for an extended period.
Persistent denial of service. Rapid repeated delivery corrupts the SQLite database behind SMS storage, turning a momentary crash into a phone that crashes on every boot (detailed below).
Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate.
From a 2-second crash to a bricked phone: the SQLite race
A single message is a repeated transient outage. Sending the payload rapidly in succession (≈30 messages) is materially worse: the crashes interleave with the telephony provider's writes to the SMS store and hit a race condition that corrupts the SQLite database holding the device's messages.
Once the database is corrupt, com.android.phone no longer needs a fresh message to fail: it crashes immediately on every boot as it reads the damaged store. The phone is now persistently without telephony, and a restart does not clear it.
Recovery is hostile, and this is the critical part: a factory reset only helps temporarily, because the carrier re-sends the unacknowledged payload and re-triggers the crash. Full recovery required:
Removing the physical SIM and inserting it into a non-Android device (e.g. an iPhone) so the carrier's retried messages are acknowledged and stop being redelivered;
Then clearing the SMS records / corrupt database over ADB.
On a device using an eSIM, where the SIM can't simply be moved to another handset, recovery would be significantly harder, and for a non-technical user, effectively out of reach.
This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service requiring a factory reset (and more) to recover, which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's own rules.
03 / Why this is serious
A remote attacker can cut a phone off from Triple Zero
Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or bricked by the SQLite corruption, it cannot reliably place a call to 000. The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing.
Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination, administered by the ACMA, carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset. Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days.
The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to cut it off the network, not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until a fix exists. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand.
The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces.
Sources: ACMA: proposed amendments to the ECS Determination · Telstra: Emergency Call Service Determination · Dept. of PM&C: impact analysis
04 / The fix
One bounds check
The remedy is a range check before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (line 217), provided to Google on the day of the first report:
long rawHeaderLen = pduDecoder.getValue32();
if (rawHeaderLen < 0 || rawHeaderLen > pdu.length) {
    result.statusCode = Intents.RESULT_SMS_GENERIC_ERROR;
    return result;
}
int headerLength = (int) rawHeaderLen;
05 / Disclosure timeline
Communication with Google
The report was filed through the Android & Google Devices VRP and resubmitted twice as a mis-triage appeal. Across three tickets and four engineers, Google classified it as a non-security issue.
Researcher
Android Security Team
Status change
5 May 2026Researcher
Report filed: zero-click WAP Push crash in WapPushOverSms (issue 509520497). Suggested fix provided the same day.
5 May 2026Android Security
Assigned for investigation; researcher asked to follow coordinated disclosure.
15 May 2026Researcher
Requests higher priority: reproduced on 5 handsets, emergency-call impact, Australian carrier regulations.
20 Jun 2026Android Security
Closed Won't Fix (Infeasible): "not a security vulnerability."
20 Jun 2026Researcher
Clarifies this is a remote permanent DoS; ~20 messages permanently disable the phone. Resubmits as appeal (issues 525810560 and 525816147, "SMS of DEATH").
20 Jun 2026Android Security
Resubmit 525810560 closed within 3 minutes Won't Fix (Not Reproducible).
22 Jun 2026Researcher
Reports SQLite corruption from rapid sends → crash on boot; recovery needs SIM swap to a non-Android device + ADB.
23 Jun 2026Android Security
Requests disclosure plans; reminds of the 90-day VRP timeline and asks to review any write-up in advance.
23 Jun 2026Researcher
Agrees to hold for public safety; offers to brief Australian carriers so they can schedule a block. Restates the one-line fix.
2-3 Jul 2026Android Security
Appeal marked Duplicate of the original; re-evaluation confirms same root cause.
16 Jul 2026Android Security
Original reopened after the issue surfaced on Discord, then confirmed a duplicate again.
16 Jul 2026Researcher
Adds detail: the behaviour meets the VRP's own "Destructive Remote DoS" criterion.
17 Jul 2026Android Security
Acknowledges the extra context; triage to take another look: "4 engineers will have evaluated the report."
27 Oct 2026Researcher
Requests a status update after three months of silence.
29 Oct 2026Android Security
Final decision: Won't Fix, quoting "does not meet the severity threshold ... considered a Non-Security Issue (NSI)."
Why this is public. The issue was reported privately and held well beyond the VRP's 90-day window. Google declined to fix it across three tickets and four engineers, classifying a remote, zero-click, emergency-call-dropping denial of service as a non-security issue. Full disclosure follows so that users, carriers and downstream OEMs can assess the risk and mitigate.
06 / Proof of concept
Source & APK
The proof-of-concept Android app and full source code are published on GitHub. The app crafts the malformed WAP Push PDU and sends it as a data SMS to a target number.
Warning: this is a working weapon. The repository contains a proof-of-concept that can remotely disrupt and brick mobile phones. It is published strictly for security research, education, and defensive testing.
Only run it against devices you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Using it against anyone else is a crime, and interfering with a person's ability to reach emergency services (000) is a serious criminal offence in Australia and most countries.
The software is provided "as is", with no warranty, under the Apache License 2.0. The author accepts no liability for any use, misuse, or damage. By downloading the APK or the source, you accept full responsibility for what you do with it.
Download APK
Source on GitHub
Full disclosure by Mark B · LinkedIn
