// MIT License Click to show
// Fast floor division by 86400.
// (rounds towards negative infinity).
// Accurate over the full signed 64-bit range.
// Sign-selected multiplier variant.
// Optional ref:
// https://www.benjoffe.com/fast-floordiv#fn=i64_86400
inline int64_t fast_i64_floordiv_86400(int64_t x) {
  const int64_t M = ((__int128(1) << 79) / 86400 + 1);
  const int64_t m = M + (x >> 63);
  return (__int128) x * m >> 79;
}
For the avoidance of doubt, the license only applies if you copy/paste the comment and code verbatim. No license is required if you re-write the same logic in your code.
Testing
A set of 65535 divisors from -32768 to 32767 for 64-bit can be generated into a single self-contained C++ file. It includes a boundary test in the same file.
See the comment at the top of the download for how to build and run it.
⬇ Download 64-bit Functions + Test
STARTING WITH TRUNCATED (STANDARD) DIVISION
DEEP LINK
Let's suppose you want to convert a Unix timestamp measured in seconds, to rata-die (a day count). And let's also suppose you forgot how to do this properly, and you use standard ("truncated") division.
We need to divide by 86400 (60×60×24). We'll use a 64-bit timestamp, since a 32-bit timestamp can only hold about ±68 years.
You'll be very happy with this implementation on the right until somebody hands you a timestamp before 1970!
C++ Standard Division (not floor-div)
Given: x — signed 64-bit integer
const int64_t rd = x / 86400;
return rd;
The above function returns incorrect results for most negative values.
Of course, you should be using floor division, the type of division that's useful for tracking repeating patterns like timestamps, angle rotations, tile positions etc. This is the type of division where the associated "%" operation is a proper positive modulus, not that fake modulus that "%" provides in C++, JavaScript etc.
Nonetheless, it's useful to understand what is going on under the hood when doing standard division like this. The pseudocode to the right shows what the compiled assembly is actually doing. It's essentially a mul‑shift and bump-by-1 for negatives.
Standard Division Compiled Steps (pseudocode)
const i64 M = (i128(1) << 77) / 86400 + 1 // Precomputed
const i128 wide = i128(x) * M
const i64  tbit = wide >> 77      // high64(wide) >> 13
const i64  sign = u64(x) >> 63   // ts < 0 ? 1 : 0
return tbit + sign
x86-64 Latency Steps
Step Computation 1 Computation 2
1 wide = ts * M
2 mul-latency sign = u64(ts) >> 63
3 mul-latency
4 high64bits(wide) >> 13
5 ... + sign
If you haven't bit twiddled much, the step u64(ts) >> 63 might seem odd. This is just moving the highest-bit down to the bottom. Since the top bit is the sign-bit on 2's complement computers, this leaves a 1 for negative numbers and a 0 for positive numbers.
Aside on Uncooperative Divisors
Deep link
Btw, if you're new to all this, you might think: "Great! I now understand how signed division works at the compiler level!"
Sorry to burst the bubble, but here's what the same thing looks like for 64-bit division by 100:
Divide by 100 (C++)
Given: x — signed 64-bit integer
return x / 100;
Divide by 100 low level steps (pseudocode)
Given: x — signed 64-bit integer
const i64 M = (i128(1) << 70) / 100 + 1
const i128 wide = i128(x) * M
const i64 tbit = ((wide >> 64) + x) >> 6
const i64 sign = u64(x) >> 63
return tbit + sign
You should notice we now have some extra junk in there: ((wide >> 64) + x) >> 6.
This is required because the magic multiplier for 100 happens to require all 64-bits for M.
This causes the top bit to be 1, making M a negative number, and as computed, the value of M ends up2^64 lower than it should be. Since we compute x * M, the value of wide is thus 2^64 * x lower than it should be. By adding x to the upper-register of the wide double-register result, we correct for it perfectly.
Divisors that require these corrections are referred to by some authors as uncooperative divisors.
x86-64 Latency Steps
Step Computation 1 Computation 2
1 wide = x * M
2 mul-latency sign = u64(x) >> 63
3 mul-latency
4 high64bits(wide) + x
5 ... >> 6
6 ... + sign
The main takeaway here is that regular division is usually the cost of around 1 multiplication + 2-3 cycles.
FIXING THE BUG
DEEP LINK
Okay, back to div 86400; you get bitten by the bug, and decide to patch it. It's pretty clear that the bug can occur when x < 0, but not always. If it's negative and divisible by 86400, it still works.
So therefore, it needs adjusting when rem < 0, like so:
But you think to yourself, surely there must be a faster way? Computing the modulus is almost as expensive as the division itself, and it gets thrown away after the bump in our theoretical use-case.
The 2nd example to the right is perhaps the first simplification that may come to mind, but it's actually slower! You can visit the Godbolt link to see that it produces more assembly lines...
C++
const int64_t div = x / 86400;
const int64_t rem = x % 86400;
return div - (rem < 0);
C++ (attractive, but slower)
Godbolt (this and above) 
const int64_t div = x / 86400;
return div - (div * 86400 > x);
Okay, screw this unintuitive nonsense, let's Google "fast floor division in c++", and get an AI summary like this (cached PDF export).
This AI summary is very misleading, as it falsely claims "Here are the fastest, branchless methods for each scenario.", before presenting a constant floor division routine that is no better than our attempt here, despite faster ways being known for 30 years+ (although it handles negative divisors at least).
In any case, the code to the right is what it suggests.
At least now we can have a flexible utility function, and it seems GCC and Clang can compile this into the same assembly as our previous version when the divisor is hard-coded (see on Godbolt ).
This is basically the same function used by Java Math.floorDiv , Python's numpy , Zig , Ruby and many other libraries.
Common Solution for signed divisors
Given: x, y — Signed Integers Compute x FLOOR_DIV y
const int64_t div = x / y;
const int64_t rem = x % y;
return div - (rem != 0 && (x ^ y) < 0);
WHAT HACKER'S DELIGHT HAS TO SAY ABOUT IT
DEEP LINK
Hacker's Delight, 2nd Edition, has a section listed in the table of contents: "10–12 Applicability to Modulus and Floor Division". That sounds promising!
It comes immediately after dozens of awesome pages with fancy tricks for other types of division (signed, unsigned etc.).
The entire contents of Section 10–12:
“ It might seem that turning modulus or floor division by a constant into multiplication would be simpler, in that the “add 1 if the dividend is negative” step could be omitted. This is not the case. The methods given above do not apply in any obvious way to modulus and floor division. Perhaps something could be worked out; it might involve altering the multiplier m slightly, depending upon the sign of the dividend. ”
— Henry S. Warren, Jr.,   Hacker's Delight, 2nd Edition
That's the whole section...
Normally, it might be copyright infringement to duplicate an entire section from a book, but in this case it's so short I think I'm covered by fair use.
Although Warren doesn't offer any solutions, the section highlighted in yellow perfectly predicts the new approach I'll introduce later.
FASTER TECHNIQUES
DEEP LINK
At this point, you would be forgiven in thinking this can't be optimised any further; maybe it can't for runtime divisors (I have not investigated, since I've focused mainly on compile-time). Looking further, the first Google Search result: the archaeological remains of the once bustling Stack Overflow. The title looks promising: Fast floor of a signed integer division in C / C++ .
The post is from 2017, and has 6 answers. The OP and the top five up-voted results all use variations of the above technique.
Finally, if you scroll to the bottom, you see after seven years, user ufoguy finally posts an answer that is notably faster for compile-time divisors:
"[Not] sure why this one wasn't mentioned; just one division, no modulo, branch-less:"
C++ - Floor division (where b > 0)
int floor_div(int a, int b) {
    return (a + (a < 0)) / b - (a < 0);
}
By my benchmarks this gives a neat improvement, it runs around 50% greater throughput on most devices.
What does ufoguy get for adding this?
No thanks, no up-vote, just a comment pointing out that this does not account for negative divisors.
A fair caveat. If we're going to make a fast general purpose lib, it might as well be flexible.
Luckily, the general case was solved at least as far back as the 90s.
It is documented clearly on page 6 of Division by Invariant Integers using Multiplication - Granlund, Montgomery, 1994.
Using the technique from that paper, we can create a simple flexible template function (non-zero divisor known at compile time).
I've prepared an example using that technique which can be called like this in C++: floor_div<int64_t(86400)>(timestamp);.
Note that the paper demonstrates a fully branchless version, but I prefer the one above for division by constants, as it's just blindly clear what's going on, and also given the branch is compile-time, it's guaranteed to simplify. Compilers readily recognise the repeated comparison eg. (x < 0) and reuse the result. However see a Godbolt comparison of the fully branchless version to see how MSVC struggles to simplify it.
Seems like floor-div is solved right?
We're only just getting started...
C++ Granlund Montgomery floor div (v1)
#include <type_traits>
template <auto D>
constexpr decltype(D) floor_div(decltype(D) x) {
    static_assert(std::is_integral_v<decltype(D)> &&
        std::is_signed_v<decltype(D)> && D != 0,
        "divisor must be a signed non-zero integer");
    if constexpr (D > 0)
        return (x + (x < 0)) / D - (x < 0);
    else
        return (x - (x > 0)) / D - (x > 0);
}
Code highlighted in green is compile-time only and has no runtime impact.
THE POSITIVE DIVISOR XOR TRICK
DEEP LINK
The division in the previous section was, at best, a mul-shift plus 5-6 cycles.
Why so many?
One for x < 0 (or x > 0).
One to add that to the numerator.
One to subtract that from the result.
Two or three for the division itself (remember earlier we showed division is a mul-shift + 2-3 cycles?)
Luckily for us, Granlund and Montgomery have another trick up their sleeve, but it's only specified for positive divisors:
Floor Div - Positive Fast Path (v1)
Given: D — Positive 64-bit integer
Pre-Solve: M — Magic-multiplier
Pre-Solve: S — Magic-shift
i64 s = x >> 63 // x < 0 ? -1 : 0
u64 a = x ^ s
u64 b = (u128) a * M >> S
i64 c = b ^ s
return c;
The diagram to the right is my attempt at visualising this.
It's a bit crazy!

title: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 | Alpine Linux
content:
2026-10-28
GITLAB SECURITY INCIDENT: ATTEMPTED EXPLOITATION OF CVE-2026-97229
On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with.
GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites.
If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org.
WHAT HAPPENED
The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12, but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23, in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9.
The attack: On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out.
Our upgrade didn’t fix the vulnerability: Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch.
If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later.
If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable.
INCIDENT TIMELINE
Date Event
Oct 28 GitLab rebuild complete; all passwords reset and GitLab's secret keys replaced
Oct 27 GitLab closed to everyone except developers and build servers; rebuild started
Oct 26 Found the instance still vulnerable after the upgrade
Oct 25 to 26 Attacker returns and tries to get back in; attempts fail
Oct 24 aports, packages and Oct 21 releases verified against outside records
Oct 23 Attacker's account blocked; Ruby releases the fix
Oct 22 Upgraded to GitLab 19.3.6
Oct 21 Main attack; GitLab crashes, 502 errors and failed CI jobs
Oct 20 Attacker registers an account and starts probing
Oct 13 CVE-2026-97229 published; we upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5 (which had the fix) by mistake
Oct 12 GitLab releases the fix
WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE CAN’T RULE OUT
What we found
Alpine releases and packages were not modified. The October 21 stable releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3), including their ISO images and the minirootfs tarballs the official alpine Docker images are built from, and all packages built from October 20 to 24 came from aports commits we verified against records outside GitLab. See the FAQ below for details.
No signing keys were exposed. The keys that sign Alpine packages and releases are not, and never have been, stored on the GitLab server.
No evidence that the attacker’s code ran: timing probes showed no delays, and we found no unexpected files, keys, hooks or processes.
No private data was returned to the attacker through any web or API request we can see.
Why we can’t be sure
A successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs.
Some logs from the attack day are gone (background job logs, the old container’s filesystem).
We had no logging of outbound network connections, and our hosting provider keeps none either.
What could have been exposed if the attack succeeded
Email addresses, names and IP addresses of all users
Password hashes
2FA secrets, CI/CD variables and runner tokens
Webhook, integration and push mirror credentials
Personal access tokens (stored as hashes)
Private repositories, and confidential issues and merge requests
FAQ
WHY DID WE REBUILD GITLAB IF WE WERE ABLE TO MITIGATE THE ATTACK?
Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch. This removes any foothold a possibly successful exploit could have left behind.
While GitLab is closed, our package mirrors, cgit, and mailing lists/IRC are available as normal.
ARE ALPINE PACKAGES AND RELEASES AFFECTED?
We have found no sign of tampering in aports or the releases.
Every aports commit added October 20 to 22 arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. We checked this against records the attacker could not reach: a developer’s clone and all 45 builders. Every package built from October 20 to 24, on every architecture, came from commits as published on git.alpinelinux.org. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were built from those same verified commits.
We ran these checks on October 24, covering commits from October 20 to 22 and packages built up to October 24. Our GitLab stayed vulnerable until we closed it on October 27, so we are extending the same checks to that date.
IS ALPINE’S RUBY PACKAGE AFFECTED?
The bug is in Ruby’s regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge ship Ruby 3.4.12, and Alpine 3.21 ships Ruby 3.3.13; both include the fix. Run apk upgrade to get it.
WHAT ARE WE CHANGING IN RESPONSE TO THIS EVENT?
Fixed Ruby: the rebuilt instance runs a Ruby with the fix (3.3.13 or later).
Faster patching: apply critical GitLab security releases within a day, and check each release for Ruby or other component patches our own build must apply.
Better logging: record outbound connections from the GitLab host and database connections, and keep logs longer than 14 days.
Signed release tags, so releases can be verified independently of GitLab.

title: Claude Code burns ~15-20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line: a Bun preload that turns agent_summary off · by Flamerix AI, flamerix.ai · MIT · GitHub
content:
Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off
by Flamerix AI · MIT License
Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified (BUN_OPTIONS=--preload). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify.
TL;DR
curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js
claude daemon stop --any
BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" claude
To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install.
The problem
Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default.
The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself.
query_source = agent_summary week before the hook 2 days after
share of all Claude Code spend 16.4 % (main conversation: 15.7 %) 0 %
share of all API requests 19.7 %, about 1 in 5 0 %
part of that spend on Opus 96 % —
input tokens per output token ≈ 9,000 : 1 —
Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate (cost_usd), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %.
The fix (how it works)
no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps setTimeout/setInterval; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary.
Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch. But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once.
Install
Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path.
Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. One of:
# ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc
export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
# ~/.config/fish/config.fish
set -gx BUN_OPTIONS "--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js"
# ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches
# user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login)
BUN_OPTIONS=--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js
Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another):
#!/bin/sh
HOOK=/abs/path/no-agent-summary.js
case " ${BUN_OPTIONS-} " in
  *" --preload $HOOK "*) ;;
  *) export BUN_OPTIONS="${BUN_OPTIONS:+$BUN_OPTIONS }--preload $HOOK" ;;
esac
: "${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG:=${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/tmp}/no-agent-summary.log}"
export CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG
exec /path/to/the/real/claude "$@"
Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS:
claude daemon stop --any
Env
variable values effect
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE off (default), pass off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off.
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG file path, optional Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=… on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count.
CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MARKER file path, optional Overwritten on load with the preload active … line.
Nuances
Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any.
Headless runs need it too: claude -p, cron, CI, editor integrations.
Platform: Linux tested, macOS and Windows untested. On Windows the /$bunfs/ gate most likely never installs the hook.
A/B: CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_MODE=pass loads the hook but arms every timer; the summaries come back, which shows the off result is the hook's doing.
Background processes: daemon, pty host and bg-spare must carry --preload in their environment (/proc/<pid>/environ on Linux); if not, restart the daemon.
Verify (after every update)
Preload loads:
BUN_OPTIONS="--preload $HOME/.local/share/no-agent-summary.js" CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log claude --version && cat /tmp/nas.log
Expect preload active mode=off …. No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute.
Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log, run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode.
Fail-open
Matching is by source text: an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen:
the log line or query-source id is renamed;
the callback is passed via fn.bind(...) (no source in toString) or another wrapper;
the strings move to a shared constant outside the callback;
the timer moves to an unwrapped API (timers/promises, a scheduler loop).
So re-run Verify after every update.
Effect
We run it under every Claude Code process on our machine (2.1.301). Since then there have been zero agent_summary requests, and no other side query grew to take its place.
Subagents, background agents, forked skills and background sessions run normally; only the summary fork is skipped.
Visible change: the per-agent panel status stops updating; SDK task_progress has no summary.
Overhead: one Function.prototype.toString per distinct timer callback, cached in a WeakMap. claude --version: ~10 ms → ~17 ms (one measurement).
Tested versions
Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1, one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file.
version published sha256 static summary forks in a ~2.5-min agent run: no hook / hook pass / hook off notes
2.1.312 2026-10-27 4f4178ce41d8 OK 5 / 5 / 0 latest on 2026-10-28; interactive: 6 no hook, 0 off
2.1.310 2026-10-23 b73676430af1 OK 5 / 5 / 0
2.1.308 2026-10-22 356733f185fa OK 5 / 6 / 0 stable on 2026-10-28; the pass run's agent took 9 steps instead of 8
2.1.301 2026-10-15 bc1aad9982c7 OK 5 / 5 / 0 same with earlier hook builds; interactive off also 0; in daily use since 2026-10-26, 0 agent_summary requests in telemetry
2.1.280 2026-09-22 1e08503dbdf3 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) interactive: -p cannot enable summaries on this version. The agent sat at a permission prompt, so later timers skipped the unchanged transcript
2.1.257 2026-09-01 9a64bda9d872 OK 1 / 1 / 0 (timer fired 11 / 11 / 0) same as 2.1.280
5 / 5 / 0 = the fork happens on this version, merely loading the hook changes nothing, and off removes it.
Why there is no setting for this
The documented switch only turns it on. The SDK option agentProgressSummaries defaults to false, but in the bundle it is one term of an OR, and every code path that writes it sets true. So false changes nothing, and the undocumented CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES can only enable summaries too.
The interval belongs to the server. It comes from a per-model-family server flag and is clamped to 30–240 s. The default is already the minimum, and no value disables the timer.
The obvious env vars miss. DISABLE_NON_ESSENTIAL_MODEL_CALLS, which some packagers set, does not occur in the binary at all. CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 do stop it, but only by taking fork subagents or background agents with it.
The prompt cache makes it cheaper, not cheap. About 98 % of these calls re-read the transcript from cache; the ~2 % that hit a cold cache carry over a third of its cost.
Cost tools that read transcripts don't see it. These requests are not written to the session logs on disk (#104358); only the OpenTelemetry export shows them. The docs section on background token usage doesn't list it either, while Agent View's row summaries are documented as a Haiku-class model refreshing every few minutes.
A cheaper variant already exists, switched off. 2.1.310 ships a short mode: about 2k tokens of notes instead of the full transcript, optionally written by a smaller model. The default is still the full transcript, and only server flags can change it.
Timeline (2026)
version (published) what changed
2.1.32 (Feb 5) the code first appears; dead in public builds
2.1.72 (Mar 9) reachable as an SDK opt-in
2.1.117 (Apr 21) reachable in the interactive CLI behind the fork gate or a server rollout
≤ 2.1.220 (Jul 24) forked skills are always summarized
2.1.232 (Aug 13) on by default for interactive background agents
2.1.300 (Oct 14) interval becomes server-tunable, 30–240 s
2.1.310 (Oct 23) the cheaper short mode lands, switched off
In our telemetry its weekly share of spend went from 3.5–7 % in July (the fork gate was already open for us) to 7.3 % and then 11.8 % in the week we picked up 2.1.233, and to about 16 % by mid-October.
License and disclaimer
MIT © 2026 Flamerix AI. Provided as is, without warranty of any kind; you use it at your own risk. Flamerix AI is not liable for any damage, data loss or account action arising from its use. Changing a client's runtime behaviour may conflict with the terms of the service you use it with; checking that is on you.

title: CNC Stone Carving - Carmelite Gothic
content:
CARMELITE MONKS OF WYOMING GOTHIC
GOTHIC
OUR DESIGN
PROGRESS
THE MONKS
CNC STONE CARVING
Home » CNC Stone Carving
CNC Stone Carving
In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place.  However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange.  To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head.
(The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.)
CNC carving of a Gothic pinnacle by the Carmelite Monks
CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today. 
The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God.
CNC Programing of a Gothic pinnacle by a Carmelite Monk
What is a CNC machine
CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention.
Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process.
CNC stone cutting blade and bits used by the Carmelite Monks
Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings!
CNC lathe and spindle at work carving stone for Carmelite Monks
Prussiani CNC machines
The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs.
The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the inside of the CNC milling area.  After the shock settled, we proceeded to analyze what had happened.  It turns out there was a mistake in the particular batch of code the machine had read and followed that night.  At the very end of each window sill, after it had completely finished carving, the code told the CNC machine to repeatedly pound down into the top of the sill, almost as if it was a giant fist.  The stones didn’t stand a chance, but that same machine is still carving stones to this day, almost a decade later.
The Carving Process
The process of carving stone with a CNC is a digital workflow.  The ornate pieces covered in foliage, the statues, the gargoyles, and many other distinct Gothic elements begin with the artist, the head carver.  He sculpts the various flowers and leaves using a 3d modeling program in a process much similar to molding a ball of clay.  It still requires a great deal of artistic talent, but there is a major advantage to this work in a computer, the Undo button!  The artist can experiment with an almost infinite number of designs to find the one most suited to the space.  And with the ability to visualize the pieces in a full model of the church, there is no longer any guesswork as to what the finished building will look like. 
The Brother artist carving in mudbox for the Carmelite Monks Gothic
Once the artist has finished a particular sculpture it is passed on to the actual stone carvers, the CNC programmers.  The programmers take the 3d model into a CAM program, which stands for computer aided machining, and create the toolpaths that the CNC machine will use to carve the actual stones.  Utilizing a large arsenal of tooling and methods they gradually carve the stone down to the finished piece.  They do their best to transform the stone block they start with to as close a resemblance of the artist’s model as possible, similar to the way stone carvers have historically used a pointing machine to transfer measurements from a plaster model into stone.  At the same time they have to juggle a wide array of concerns, from which tools to use depending on speed and finish, to how to keep the stone from moving, to avoiding collisions between the cnc and the stone, or even other stones they might be carving at the same time.  This is a lot to keep track of, but if done well, it will quickly bear fruit.  It is extremely rewarding to see the keystrokes and mouse clicks of a computer turn into not only a finished product, but an ornately carved part of a Gothic church, a place God will be loved for centuries to come.
Finally, once all of that Gcode (the programming language of a CNC machine) is ready, it is handed over to the sawyers, who operate the CNC machines themselves, as well as the various other saws that prepare the stone blocks for carving.  The sawyers are the “boots on the ground” guys and keep a clear line of communication open with the programmers to ensure that everything runs smoothly.  They carefully follow the layouts and tooling lists the programmers prepare for each piece as they set up the stones for carving, set reference points so the machines can locate each stone, and monitor it as it carves.  They are constantly keeping a watchful eye to ensure that everything goes smoothly.  There is a symbiotic relationship between the sawyers and the programmers as the work of each is essential to the successful completion of each stone. 
The Monk Sawyers setting up a table to be Carved for the CNC
The sawyers also operate the wire saws and bridge saws, cutting each stone to either be carved into something more ornate, or to go straight into the wall.  The wire saw, a simpler type of 2 axis cnc itself, can cut simple profiles, including any straight piece, such as columns and the straight parts of window surrounds.  The sawyer, using the wire saw, will take a large slab of stone and sometimes cut even 20 or 30 different smaller stones out of it; looking similar to pieces from a cookie cutter.  This frees up the 5 axis CNC machines to focus on the more ornate pieces, and is also significantly faster.
The monk Wire sawyer puts in plastic shims to support the cut pieces. On the right is the finished product of the wire saw awaiting the denesting of the profiled stones
There are many different facets to the art and science of stone carving today and only a few have been touched on here.  Pneumatic chisels and hand carving certainly have a valuable role to play, as well as a multitude of other methods not discussed here.  The learning curve to dive into such a work is indeed daunting, the workload intimidating, but the fruit of it will stand for centuries to come.

Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen
Andrew
on
October 26, 2026
For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand.
The problem
Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked.
Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it.
Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops.
What The Grid is
The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it.
Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines.
It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid.
What it means for a real board
To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address.
Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median.
So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165.
It's not a prototype
The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers.
What's next
Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027.
The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can.
If you want to help rebuild the Western electronics supply chain, we're hiring. And if you have a board to build, get an instant quote.

title: Introducing Gemini 4 Carbon
content:
Home
Innovation & AI
Models & research
Gemini Models
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model
Oct 28, 2026
6 min read
Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
Koray Kavukcuoglu
SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google
Share
Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.
Building on Gemini 4 Argon, which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.
We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program. We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.
Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price
1
as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.
Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks
Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.
Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena.
State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems
Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.
Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):
Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.
Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%).
Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench, turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.
Advancing frontier model safety & security
Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report. With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.
Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.
Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.
Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.
Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.
Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.
Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers
Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

Implementation
struct item {
    int key, prior;
    item *l, *r;
    item () { }
    item (int key) : key(key), prior(rand()), l(NULL), r(NULL) { }
    item (int key, int prior) : key(key), prior(prior), l(NULL), r(NULL) { }
};
typedef item* pitem;
This is our item definition. Note there are two child pointers, and an integer key (for the BST) and an integer priority (for the heap). The priority is assigned using a random number generator.
void split (pitem t, int key, pitem & l, pitem & r) {
    if (!t)
        l = r = NULL;
    else if (t->key <= key)
        split (t->r, key, t->r, r),  l = t;
    else
        split (t->l, key, l, t->l),  r = t;
}
t is the treap to split, and key is the BST value by which to split. Note that we do not return the result values anywhere; instead, the output treaps are written through l and r, for example:
pitem l = nullptr, r = nullptr;
split(t, 5, l, r);
This split function can be tricky to understand, as it has both pointers (pitem) as well as reference to those pointers (pitem &l). Let us understand in words what the function call split(t, k, l, r) intends: "split treap t by value k into two treaps, and store the left treaps in l and right treap in r". Great! Now, let us apply this definition to the two recursive calls, using the case work we analyzed in the previous section: (The first if condition is a trivial base case for an empty treap)
When the root node value is
≤
$\le$  key, we call split (t->r, key, t->r, r), which means: "split treap t->r (right subtree of t) by value key and store the left subtree in t->r and right subtree in r". After that, we set l = t. Note now that the l result value contains t->l, t as well as t->r (which is the result of the recursive call we made) all already merged in the correct order! You should pause to ensure that this result of l and r corresponds exactly with what we discussed earlier in Implementation Description.
When the root node value is greater than key, we call split (t->l, key, l, t->l), which means: "split treap t->l (left subtree of t) by value key and store the left subtree in l and right subtree in t->l". After that, we set r = t. Note now that the r result value contains t->l (which is the result of the recursive call we made), t as well as t->r, all already merged in the correct order! You should pause to ensure that this result of l and r corresponds exactly with what we discussed earlier in Implementation Description.
If you're still having trouble understanding the implementation, you should look at it inductively, that is: do not try to break down the recursive calls over and over again. Assume the split implementation works correct on empty treap, then try to run it for a single node treap, then a two node treap, and so on, each time reusing your knowledge that split on smaller treaps works.
void insert (pitem & t, pitem it) {
    if (!t)
        t = it;
    else if (it->prior > t->prior)
        split (t, it->key, it->l, it->r),  t = it;
    else
        insert (t->key <= it->key ? t->r : t->l, it);
}

void merge (pitem & t, pitem l, pitem r) {
    if (!l || !r)
        t = l ? l : r;
    else if (l->prior > r->prior)
        merge (l->r, l->r, r),  t = l;
    else
        merge (r->l, l, r->l),  t = r;
}

void erase (pitem & t, int key) {
    if (t->key == key) {
        pitem th = t;
        merge (t, t->l, t->r);
        delete th;
    }
    else
        erase (key < t->key ? t->l : t->r, key);
}

pitem unite (pitem l, pitem r) {
    if (!l || !r)  return l ? l : r;
    if (l->prior < r->prior)  swap (l, r);
    pitem lt, rt;
    split (r, l->key, lt, rt);
    l->l = unite (l->l, lt);
    l->r = unite (l->r, rt);
    return l;
}
Maintaining the sizes of subtrees
To extend the functionality of the treap, it is often necessary to store the number of nodes in subtree of each node - field int cnt in the item structure. For example, it can be used to find K-th largest element of tree in
O
(
log
⁡
N
)
$O (\log N)$ , or to find the index of the element in the sorted list with the same complexity. The implementation of these operations will be the same as for the regular binary search tree.
When a tree changes (nodes are added or removed etc.), cnt of some nodes should be updated accordingly. We'll create two functions: cnt() will return the current value of cnt or 0 if the node does not exist, and upd_cnt() will update the value of cnt for this node assuming that for its children L and R the values of cnt have already been updated. Evidently it's sufficient to add calls of upd_cnt() to the end of insert, erase, split and merge to keep cnt values up-to-date.
int cnt (pitem t) {
    return t ? t->cnt : 0;
}

void upd_cnt (pitem t) {
    if (t)
        t->cnt = 1 + cnt(t->l) + cnt (t->r);
}
Building a Treap in
O
(
N
)
$O (N)$  in offline mode
Given a sorted list of keys, it is possible to construct a treap faster than by inserting the keys one at a time which takes
O
(
N
log
⁡
N
)
$O(N \log N)$ . Since the keys are sorted, a balanced binary search tree can be easily constructed in linear time. The heap values
Y
$Y$  are initialized randomly and then can be heapified independent of the keys
X
$X$  to build the heap in
O
(
N
)
$O(N)$ .
void heapify (pitem t) {
    if (!t) return;
    pitem max = t;
    if (t->l != NULL && t->l->prior > max->prior)
        max = t->l;
    if (t->r != NULL && t->r->prior > max->prior)
        max = t->r;
    if (max != t) {
        swap (t->prior, max->prior);
        heapify (max);
    }
}

pitem build (int * a, int n) {
    // Construct a treap on values {a[0], a[1], ..., a[n - 1]}
    if (n == 0) return NULL;
    int mid = n / 2;
    pitem t = new item (a[mid], rand ());
    t->l = build (a, mid);
    t->r = build (a + mid + 1, n - mid - 1);
    heapify (t);
    upd_cnt(t);
    return t;
}
Note: calling upd_cnt(t) is only necessary if you need the subtree sizes.
The approach above always provides a perfectly balanced tree, which is generally good for practical purposes, but at the cost of not preserving the priorities that were initially assigned to each node. Thus, this approach is not feasible to solve the following problem:
acmsguru - Cartesian Tree
Given a sequence of pairs
(
x
i
,
y
i
$(x_i, y_i)$ , construct a cartesian tree on them. All
x
i
$x_i$  and all
y
$y_i$  are unique.
Note that in this problem priorities are not random, hence just inserting vertices one by one could provide a quadratic solution.
One of possible solutions here is to find for each element the closest elements to the left and to the right which have a smaller priority than this element. Among these two elements, the one with the larger priority must be the parent of the current element.
This problem is solvable with a minimum stack modification in linear time. The construction below uses the min-heap convention for priorities, unlike the max-heap convention used by the regular treap implementation above, and assumes that item is extended with a parent pointer p initialized to nullptr:
void connect(auto from, auto to) {
    vector<pitem> st;
    for(auto it: ranges::subrange(from, to)) {
        while(!st.empty() && st.back()->prior > it->prior) {
            st.pop_back();
        }
        if(!st.empty()) {
            if(!it->p || it->p->prior < st.back()->prior) {
                it->p = st.back();
            }
        }
        st.push_back(it);
    }
}

pitem build(int *x, int *y, int n) {
    vector<pitem> nodes(n);
    for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        nodes[i] = new item(x[i], y[i]);
    }
    connect(nodes.begin(), nodes.end());
    connect(nodes.rbegin(), nodes.rend());
    for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if(nodes[i]->p) {
            if(nodes[i]->p->key < nodes[i]->key) {
                nodes[i]->p->r = nodes[i];
            } else {
                nodes[i]->p->l = nodes[i];
            }
        }
    }

Human-enhanced tsunami hazard in large lakes
Muhammad Naveed Zafar
, Pierre Sabatier
, Denys Dutykh
, William Rapuc
, Raphaël Paris
, Andrea Piccin, Pascal Vuillemin & Flavio S. Anselmetti

volume

Save article

Abstract
Worldwide, human-induced erosion enhances sediment delivery to lake deltas, increasing their susceptibility to collapse. In Lake Iseo, northern Italy, two millennia of intensified land use tripled sediment flux, oversteepening the delta and preconditioning it for failure. Here we show from geological records and numerical simulations that earthquakes in 1117 CE (Mw 6.5) and 1222 CE (Mw 6.0) triggered major subaqueous delta collapses, generating massive tsunamis with maximum run-ups of ~50 m and ~13 m, respectively. Historical accounts from the Vatican Library and archeological evidence support these reconstructions. Since the last collapse, eight centuries of human-induced erosion have rebuilt the delta, leaving shoreline populations highly vulnerable to future earthquake-triggered failures. A global lake synthesis showed that human-driven erosion has reached its highest levels since the Industrial Era, progressively overloading deltas worldwide; thus, similar catastrophic failures may become more likely in the future. These findings reveal a persistent, human-amplified mechanism of lacustrine tsunami generation and intensity with major implications for hazard assessment.
